Dosage form/formulation	INJECTION, POWDER, LYOPHILIZED, FOR SOLUTION
Dosing regimen	Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia (SAB) in Adults:
667 mg every 6 hours on day 1 to 8, followed by every 8 hours from day 9 onwards over 2-hour infusion
ABSSSI and CABP in Adults: 667 mg every 8 hours over 2 hour infusion
CABP in Pediatric Patients:
Adolescents: 12 to less than 18 years of age: 13.3 mg/kg (up to 667 mg) every 8 hours over 2-hour infusion
Infants and children: 3 months and less than 12 years old: (b)(4) mg/kg (up to 667 mg) every 8 hours over 2 hour infusion
Note: 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole. For pediatric patients: 13.3 mg/kg is equivalent to 10 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. (b)(4) mg/kg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to (b)(4) mg/kg of ceftobiprole. Dosing adjustments for each indication are based on renal function
L7: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L8: Applicant-proposed indications/populations	
1. Treatment of adult patients with Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection (bacteremia) (SAB), including those with right-sided infective endocarditis, caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin resistant isolates.
2. Treatment of adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae(b) (4) and Klebsiella pneumoniae.
3. Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (greater than or equal to 3 months to less than 18 years of age) with CABP caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus(b) (4) isolates), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae

SNOMED CT code for proposed indication disease term(s)1	406602003 |Infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus (disorder)|
128936008 |Bacterial infection of skin (disorder)|
385093006 |Community acquired pneumonia (disorder)|
Regulatory action	Approval
Approved dosage	See Tables below
Dosing in Adults
Indicationa	Dose	Frequency
SAB	667 mgb	Every 6 hours on Days 1 to 8
Every 8 hours from Day 9
ABSSSI	667 mgb	Every 8 hours
CABP	667 mgb	Every 8 hours
L9: aDuration of treatment in adult patients is up to 42 days for SAB and 5 days to 14 days for ABSSSI and CABP
L10: b 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole. b 13.3 mg/kg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 10 mg/kg of ceftobiprole; 20 mg/kg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 15 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. 667 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole.
L11: Dosing adjustments based on renal function.
L12: ## Dosing in Pediatric Patients 3 Months to Less Than 18 Years Old

3 months to less than 12 years old	20 mg/kg (up to 667 mg/doseb)	Every 8 Hours
L14: aDuration of treatment for CABP in pediatric patients is 7 days to 14 days.
L15: b 13.3 mg/kg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 10 mg/kg of ceftobiprole; 20 mg/kg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 15 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. 667 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole.

L17: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L18: Approved indications/ populations	
1. Treatment of adult patients with Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection (bacteremia), including those with right-sided infective endocarditis, caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates
2. Treatment of adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
3. Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae

L82: ## I. Executive Summary
L83: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L84: New drug application (NDA) 218275 for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection was submitted by Basilea Pharmaceutica International Ltd, Allschwil (Applicant) for the following indications:
L85: - Treatment of adult patients with *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteremia (SAB), including those with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE)
- Treatment of adult patients with acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI)
- Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (greater than or equal to 3 months to less than 18 years of age) with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP)
L86: The application was reviewed by the multidisciplinary review team. The review team has recommended approval, and I, the signatory for this application, concur with this recommendation.
L87: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug which exerts its antibacterial activity by binding to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibiting synthesis of the bacterial cell wall. Ceftobiprole medocaril is the prodrug that rapidly converts to its active moiety, ceftobiprole. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is the salt form of ceftobiprole medocaril; ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is used interchangeably with ceftobiprole throughout this review. Ceftobiprole demonstrated in vitro and clinical activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria including methicillin-susceptible *S. aureus* (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA), *Streptococcus pyogenes*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Haemophilus parainfluenzae*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and *Escherichia coli*.
L88: The Applicant submitted a single, phase 3, randomized, double-blinded, active-controlled, noninferiority trial in adults for each of the indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) that demonstrated noninferiority to the comparators. Additionally, the Applicant submitted a phase 3, randomized, active-controlled trial in pediatric subjects with CABP and hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia (HABP) and a phase 3 trial in adults with HABP and ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (VABP). Data from the pediatric CABP/HABP trial were primarily used to support the safety of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects with CABP with efficacy extrapolated from the adult CABP trial. Indications for HABP/VABP in adults and HABP in pediatric subjects were not sought in this application and the data from the HABP/VABP subjects informed safety assessments.
L89: The safety database consisted of 464 subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole in phase 1 studies, and 1315 total subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole at the to-be-marketed dose in the phase 3 trials. Overall, the safety findings observed with ceftobiprole were similar to other FDA-approved cephalosporins. The risks can be mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
L90: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L91: The overall benefit-risk profile is favorable to support approval of ceftobiprole for the treatment of:
L92: - Adult patients with SAB, including those with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE), caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates
- Adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: *Staphylococcus aureus* (methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates), *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
- Adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with CABP caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: *Staphylococcus aureus* (methicillin-susceptible), *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Haemophilus parainfluenzae*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
L93: The drug product established name and strength will be expressed in terms of the salt (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling will include a statement stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole (the active metabolite). This is an exception to the USP Salt Policy to eliminate having three different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and harmonizing the US FDA labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries.
L94: For detailed information supporting the basis for this approval, please refer to the reviews included in this interdisciplinary assessment and the product quality review.
L95: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L96: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L97: **Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework for Treatment of *Staphylococcus aureus* Bacteremia**
L98: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	Staphylococcus aureus can cause invasive infections, sepsis and death. In 2017, nearly 120,000 bloodstream infections occurred with 20,000 associated deaths. S. aureus is an ongoing threat with community-onset methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) infections increasing (3.9% per year, p<0.0001) from 2012 to 2017 (CDC 2019). Due to significant attempts to reduce MRSA bloodstream infections in healthcare settings, these infections had been decreasing by 17.1% each year from 2005 to 2012; however, no significant change was detected from 2013 to 2016.
MRSA bacteremia has a higher mortality rate than MSSA bacteremia; one meta-analysis showed an odds ratio of 1.93 (95% CI, 1.54-2.42) for in-hospital mortality compared with MSSA bacteremia. (Cosgrove et al. 2003).
RIE accounts for 5-10% of all IE cases. The most common cause of RIE is S. aureus, which accounts for an estimated 60-90% of cases and often requires 4-6 weeks of antibacterial drug therapy (Liu et al. 2011)
Bacteremia due to S. aureus remains a common cause of bloodstream infection with morbidity and mortality rates of up to 25%. IE is commonly caused by S. aureus, and native valve S. aureus endocarditis is often associated with a higher mortality as compared to other pathogens (Miro et al. 2005).
Current treatment options	FDA-approved treatments for SAB, especially MRSA bacteremia, are limited.
Treatment for SAB and RIE caused by MSSA include cefazolin, nafcillin, oxacillin, and daptomycin. Vancomycin can be used in patients with beta-lactam allergy or in those who cannot receive other drugs.
There are fewer treatment options for SAB and RIE caused by MRSA; only vancomycin and daptomycin are approved for these indications.
Limitations of vancomycin include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, and the need for therapeutic drug monitoring.
Limitations of daptomycin include myalgias, rhabdomyolysis and eosinophilic pneumonia.
Approved treatment options for MRSA bacteremia and RIE are limited by toxicity and resistance necessitating the development of antibacterial drugs with improved adverse effect profiles.
L99: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Benefit	Resistance to both vancomycin and daptomycin have been observed (McGuinness et al. 2017; Ernst and Peschel 2019).
A phase 3, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, multi-center trial in adult hospitalized subjects with SAB, including RIE was conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin \pm aztreonam (the comparator arm) for the primary endpoint of overall success at the post-treatment evaluation (PTE) visit at Day 70 after randomization in the mITT population that included subjects who received any dose of study medication, and had a blood culture positive for S. aureus at baseline. Overall success assessed by the data review committee (DRC) was defined as all of the following criteria being met: subject alive at Day 70, no new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection, resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms and two negative blood cultures for S. aureus at prespecified time points. The specified noninferiority margin was 15%. Key secondary endpoints included all-cause mortality (ACM) through PTE.
The ceftobiprole arm had an overall success rate of 69.8% (132/189); the comparator arm had an overall success rate of 68.7% (136/198); the difference (95% CI) was 2.0% (-7.1, 11.1), and the results of overall success at the PTE visit in the mITT population met the threshold for noninferiority.
All-cause mortality (ACM) through the Day 70 PTE visit in the mITT population was 9.0% (17/189) and 9.1% (18/198) in the ceftobiprole and comparator arms, respectively.
Additional analysis considered overall success at the PTE visit by pathogen. For MSSA, the overall success rates in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator arms were 70.9% (100/141) vs. 66.4% (97/146), respectively [difference (95% CI): 4.8 (-5.9, 15.5)]. For MRSA, the overall success rates in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator arms were 68.8% (31/45) vs. 77.6% (38/49), respectively [difference (95% CI): -8.3 (-25.3, 8.6)]. Of note, the microbiological eradication rates for MRSA at PTE in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator arms were 80.0% vs. 81.6%, respectively.
Overall success in subjects with definite RIE was similar between treatment arms [66.7% vs. 70% in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator arm, respectively, the difference (95% CI) was -6.6 (-40.1, 27.0)].
The phase 3 trial met its primary objective of demonstrating non-inferiority for the pre-specified primary endpoint of overall success based on DRC Assessment at the PTE (Day 70) visit. Outcomes of the secondary efficacy endpoints were similar between treatment arms.
Overall, low ethnic/geographic diversity and differences in success rates by geographic region are not anticipated to significantly limit the efficacy assessment of ceftobiprole for SAB; these differences will be described in the labeling.
Ceftobiprole provides an additional option for treatment of SAB, including RIE caused by both methicillin susceptible and methicillin resistant isolates.
L100: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Of note, overall success rates (ceftobiprole vs. comparator) based on DRC assessment at PTE in the Ukraine were: 74/88 (84.1%) vs. 82/92 (89.1%), respectively, versus 58/101 (57.4%) vs. 54/106 (50.9%), respectively, in other countries excluding the Ukraine.
Additionally, low racial and geographic diversity (96% were White and 93% were European) was observed in the trial.

Risk and risk management	The safety database included 191 subjects who received the proposed dose and duration of ceftobiprole.
Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) leading to death were similar in both treatment arms (approximately 9%). The deaths appeared to be related to underlying comorbidities and unrelated to ceftobiprole.
The incidence of SAEs was similar in the ceftobiprole arm and the daptomycin \pm aztreonam arm (18.8% vs 22.7%).
The number of subjects who had TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation was comparable in each arm (approximately 9%). The most common adverse reactions leading to treatment discontinuation were gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, and urticaria.
The most common adverse reactions occurring in \ge 4% of ceftobiprole-treated subjects were anemia, nausea, hypokalemia, vomiting, hepatic enzyme and bilirubin increased, diarrhea, blood creatinine increased, and leukopenia.
Adverse events of special interest such as hypersensitivity reactions and seizures were both reported in 1.6% of subjects.
Thrombi formation at the injection site were seen in nonclinical studies, possibly due to mechanical irritation and higher concentrations of ceftobiprole than administered in clinical trials. In the SAB trial, thrombosis-related adverse events were reported in 5% of subjects in the ceftobiprole arm and 2% of subjects in the comparator arm. Thrombosis also occurred at a low frequency (1.6%) in other clinical trials. In all clinical trials, the majority of subjects with thromboses had underlying risk factors and thrombosis has not been reported in the postmarketing setting.
The safety profile of ceftobiprole appears acceptable in subjects with SAB. The TEAEs experienced in the study are generally compatible with the known safety profile of the cephalosporin drug class.
The risks of ceftobiprole have been communicated in labeling. The Warning and Precautions section of the labeling will include hypersensitivity reactions and seizures and other central nervous system reactions. Monitoring for TEAEs of special interest will continue in the postmarketing phase.

L102: Table 3. Benefit Risk Framework for Treatment of Acute Bacterial Skin/Soft Tissue Infection
L103: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	The FDA Guidance for Industry (Acute Bacterial Skin and Skin structure Infections: Developing Drugs for Treatment) defines an ABSSSI as a bacterial infection of the skin with a lesion size of at least 75 cm2 and encompass diseases such as cellulitis/erysipelas, wound infections, and major cutaneous abscesses (October 2013).
ABSSSI are one of the most commonly diagnosed infectious diseases and account for an estimated 10.1% of all infectious disease-related hospitalizations (Christensen et al. 2009).
Treatment of cellulitis is usually directed towards the most common pathogens such as S. aureus and group A Streptococcus because the causative pathogen is rarely isolated. However, given the increased prevalence of community-associated MRSA, empiric therapy for MRSA may be considered (Chira and Miller 2010).
While gram-positive organisms are the predominant pathogens, the incidence of gram-negative organisms causing skin and soft tissue infections are on the rise (Jabbour and Kanj 2021).
ABSSSI are one of the most commonly diagnosed infectious diseases and are usually caused by S. aureus and group A Streptococcus but can be also caused by gram-negative bacteria.
Current treatment options	While there are numerous treatment options for MSSA, Streptococcus pyogenes, and group A streptococcus, there are fewer options for treating MRSA. For MRSA infection, treatment options may include vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, dalbavancin, oritavancin, ceftaroline, clindamycin, tigecycline, omadacycline, doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and delafloxacin.
There are currently numerous treatments for K. pneumonia which include but are not limited to cephalosporins, \beta-lactams/\beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, and fluoroquinolones.
Some treatment options are associated with toxicity or drug-drug interactions.
A single treatment option that combines MRSA and gram-negative antibacterial coverage may be useful in certain clinical settings.
Benefit	A phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multicenter trial in adult hospitalized subjects with ABSSSI was conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole was noninferior to vancomycin and aztreonam for the primary endpoint of early clinical response based on percent reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48-72 hours after start of treatment, measured in subjects who did not receive rescue therapy, and were alive. The primary analysis was conducted in the (Intent-to-treat) ITT
The study met its primary objective of demonstrating non-inferiority. Secondary efficacy findings also favor ceftobiprole vs. vancomycin plus aztreonam. Ceftobiprole provides an additional option for treatment of ABSSSI caused by Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible

L106: Table 4. Benefit-Risk Framework for Treatment of Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia
L107: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) is generally defined as an infection of the lung parenchyma in patients without recent healthcare exposure. The microbiology of CABP typically includes S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. pneumoniae, S. aureus, and Enterobacteriales. The rise in the incidence of antibacterial resistance necessitates the use of broader spectrum antibacterial drugs for treatment. Despite treatment, CABP continues to have significant morbidity and mortality with mortality rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.5% depending on the severity at presentation, age, co-morbidities, and level of care required (Fine et al. 1996, Peters et al. 2022) (Fine et al. 1996; Peters et al. 2022)).
Community-acquired pneumonia, both bacterial and viral, is the most common cause of death in children under 5 years of age globally, causing nearly 15% of deaths in this age group (World Health Organization). In the US, CABP is among the most common causes of hospitalization in children of all ages with an annual incidence rate of approximately 15.7 hospitalizations per 10,000 children (Jain et al. 2016)(Jain et al. 2015).
In both adults and children, CABP is a serious infection that causes significant morbidity and mortality and may be caused by a variety of pathogens.
Current treatment options	Initial treatment of CABP is empiric and is tailored to risk factors and severity of illness at presentation. FDA approved antibacterial drugs include beta-lactams, cephalosporins, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones with oral and parenteral formulations.
In pediatric patients, treatment of mild to moderate CABP in the outpatient setting involves empiric coverage of the most common causative organism, S. pneumoniae. For hospitalized patients, use of ampicillin demonstrates similar outcomes when compared to broader regimens (Messinger et al. 2017), but additional antibacterial coverage including cephalosporins and macrolides are recommended in patients with history of allergic reactions, recent influenza infection, or history of infection with MDR organisms.
There are many antibacterial drugs approved for treatment of CABP. However, with increasing antibacterial resistance, adverse reactions, including hypersensitivity, treatment options may be limited in some patients.
Benefit	A phase 3 randomized, double-blind, active control, multicenter study conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole in adult subjects diagnosed with CABP requiring
The submitted evidence showed non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to ceftriaxone \pm linezolid.
L108: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
hospitalization found that ceftobiprole demonstrated noninferiority to ceftriaxone \pm linezolid on the primary endpoint of clinical cure defined as the resolution of signs and symptoms of infection or improvement to such an extent that no further antimicrobial therapy was necessary and improvement/stabilization of chest X-ray findings with a pre-specified noninferiority margin of 15%.
The overall clinical cure rate was 86.6% for ceftobiprole compared with the overall clinical cure rate of 87.4% for the comparator group with a difference of -0.8%, 95% CI (-6.9, 5.3). The clinical cure rate in the ITT analysis was similar with 76.4% in the ceftobiprole group compared with 79.3% in the comparator group with a difference of -2.9%, 95% CI (-9.3, 3.6).
A post-hoc analysis using the currently recommend efficacy endpoint of clinical success at Day 3 confirmed that ceftobiprole was noninferior to the comparator.
Pediatrics: A phase 3, randomized, investigator blind, active control, multicenter study was conducted to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and efficacy of ceftobiprole in 138 pediatric subjects aged 3 months to < 18 years requiring hospitalization and IV antibacterial drugs for the treatment of CABP (vs. ceftriaxone \pm vancomycin) and HABP (vs. ceftazidime \pm vancomycin) with the primary objective of evaluating safety. Although the trial included subjects with both HABP and CABP, only 8 enrolled subjects had HABP. The Applicant is not seeking an indication for HABP.
A total of 94 subjects received ceftobiprole. Efficacy for CABP was extrapolated from the successful phase 3 CABP adult study described above.
Efficacy in the pediatric population was extrapolated from the adult trial.
Ceftobiprole provides an additional option for treatment of CABP caused by Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae.
L109: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Risk and risk management	In the adult CABP study, there were 9 deaths in each treatment arm (2.8%). The deaths appeared to be related to underlying comorbidities and did not appear to be related to ceftobiprole.
Approximately 11.3% of subjects treated with ceftobiprole developed an SAE and 5.5% of subjects discontinued treatment due to an AE. These rates were similar to those observed in the comparator arm.
The most common adverse reactions occurring in ≥ 2% of ceftobiprole treated subjects were nausea, hepatic enzyme increased, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, rash, insomnia, abdominal pain, phlebitis, and dizziness.
No additional safety concerns were identified in this study.
No safety concerns were identified in the pediatric study. There were no deaths. Although a numerically greater number of subjects had SAEs in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator groups (7.9% vs 4.9%, respectively) and discontinued drug due to AEs (4.5% vs. 0, respectively), only hypersensitivity and urticaria in two subjects appeared related to ceftobiprole.
Occurrence of TEAEs was balanced between treatment groups (31.5% vs. 29.3% in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator groups, respectively). The most common adverse reactions occurring in ≥ 2% of ceftobiprole treated subjects were vomiting, headache, hepatic enzyme increased, diarrhea, infusion site reaction, phlebitis, and pyrexia.
The safety profile of ceftobiprole appears acceptable as a treatment for CABP. The TEAEs experienced in the adult and pediatric studies are compatible with the known safety profile of the cephalosporin drug class. The identified safety issues can be adequately addressed by labeling.
L110: Abbreviations: AE, adverse event; CABP, community-acquired bacterial pneumonia; CI, confidence interval; HABP, hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia; ITT, intent-to-treat; REMS, risk evaluation and mitigation strategy; SAE, serious adverse event; TEAE, treatment-emergent adverse event
L111: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L112: All three of the proposed indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) are serious and often life-threatening infections with significant morbidity and mortality. While there are multiple antibacterial drugs currently approved to treat ABSSSI and CABP, the continued evolution of antibacterial resistance mechanisms, drug-drug interactions, and adverse effects of available antibacterial drugs can limit treatment options. There is an urgent need to develop antibacterial drugs which cover both gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, especially MRSA, which is a major cause of hospital and community-acquired infections worldwide. Current treatments for MRSA infections have certain limitations (e.g., vancomycin is associated with nephrotoxicity and the need for drug monitoring, linezolid has certain drug-drug interactions and toxicities, daptomycin does not penetrate the lung parenchyma, and ceftaroline is not FDA-approved for difficult to treat infections such as bacteremia and RIE). Approved treatments for SAB, including RIE due to MRSA are especially limited.
L113: Ceftobiprole, an advanced generation cephalosporin antibacterial drug would provide an effective treatment option with a favorable safety profile for the indications sought (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP). The Applicant submitted data demonstrating safety and effectiveness for all three indications.
L114: Trial BPR-CS-009 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to daptomycin \pm aztreonam in the treatment of subjects with SAB, including those with RIE, caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates in regard to the primary endpoint of overall success based on data review committee assessment at the post-treatment evaluation visit in the modified intent-to-treat population (ceftobiprole 69.8%, daptomycin 68.7% [difference 2.0%; 95% confidence interval (CI): -7.1, 11.1]), which met the prespecified 15% noninferiority (NI) margin.
L115: Trial BPR-CS-008 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in the treatment of subjects with ABSSSI with respect to the primary endpoint of early clinical response in the intent-to-treat population (ceftobiprole 91.3%, vancomycin plus aztreonam 88.1% [difference 3.3%; 95% CI: -1.2, 7.8]), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin.
L116: Trial CAP-3001 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to ceftriaxone \pm linezolid in the treatment of adult subjects with CABP. In the intent-to-treat population, the clinical cure rate in the ceftobiprole group was 76.4% compared with the comparator group at 79.3% with a treatment difference of -2.9%, 95 CI (-9.3, 3.6), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin. Efficacy for CABP in the pediatric population was extrapolated from the adult CABP Trial.
L117: The safety database for ceftobiprole was adequate for the proposed dosing regimens, intended subject populations, and respective indications. Generally, the Applicant provided data demonstrating that the safety of ceftobiprole was similar to the active comparator in each trial. Overall, ceftobiprole has a favorable safety profile, and safety findings can be adequately addressed in labeling and by routine pharmacovigilance.
L118: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L119: Based on review of all available efficacy and safety data, NDA 218275 for ceftobiprole provides substantial evidence of effectiveness and a favorable benefit-risk profile for the treatment of the following indications:
L120: - Treatment of adult patients with SAB, including those with right-sided infective endocarditis, caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates
- Treatment of adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: *Staphylococcus aureus* (methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates), *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
- Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with CABP caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: *Staphylococcus aureus* (methicillin-susceptible isolates), *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Haemophilus parainfluenzae*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*
L121: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L122: ## 3. Introduction
L123: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection (Zevtera) is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug that binds to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits their transpeptidase activity. The active ingredient (drug substance), ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, is a salt of a prodrug, ceftobiprole medocaril, and the active metabolite is ceftobiprole. The dosage form of the drug product is a powder for injection. Ceftobiprole is currently approved in several countries outside of the US for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia (HABP).
L124: Ceftobiprole was submitted under new drug application (NDA) 022132 for treatment of complicated skin and skin structure infections by the previous Applicant, Johnson and Johnson Pharmaceutical Research &amp; Development LLC (J&amp;J) on May 18, 2007. NDA 022132 received an Approvable Letter on March 17, 2008, a Complete Response Letter on November 21, 2008, and a Complete Response Letter on December 28, 2009. The Clinical Deficiencies cited in these letters concerned studies BAP 00154 and BAP 00414 which are not included in this new NDA 218275. Ownership of NDA 022132 was transferred back to Basilea Pharmaceutica Ltd. on January 24, 2011.
L125: Ceftobiprole medocaril for injection was granted Qualified Infectious Disease Product designation for the CABP, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI), and *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteremia (SAB) indications on July 20, 2015, August 7, 2015, and December 8, 2017, respectively. Refer to Section 12 for a more detailed regulatory summary.
L126: In this NDA submission, the proposed indications are for the treatment of adult patients with SAB, including right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE), ABSSSI, and CABP and for treatment of pediatric patients 3 months to less than 18 years old with CABP. For current available therapies and typical pathogens for each indication, refer to Section 2.1.
L127: All three indications were supported by phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active controlled noninferiority (NI) trials which met their respective primary endpoints within the prespecified NI margins. Refer to Section 6 and 7 for reviews of efficacy and safety for each trial.
L128: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L129: The proposed dosing regimen is ceftobiprole 500 mg every 6 hours on Days 1 to 8, followed by every 8 hours from Day 9 up to 42 days for SAB and 500 mg every 8 hours for 5 to 14 days for ABSSSI and CABP with dosing adjustments based on renal function. The initial proposal by the Applicant was based on the strength of the amount of the “active moiety/metabolite” as 500 mg ceftobiprole/vial.
L130: During the NDA review, the OPQ team recommended that the drug product established name and strength be revised following the USP Salt Policy to express the amount of the prodrug neutral form (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril for injection, 646 mg/vial). In response, the Applicant requested exemption from the USP Salt Policy following the example of a previously approved product which was also a salt of a prodrug, Cresemba (isavuconazonium sulfate), for which the strength is expressed in terms of the salt in approved labeling.
L131: The clinical team and the Division of Medication and Error Prevention Analysis (DMEPA) agreed with the Applicant that an exception to the USP Salt Policy would eliminate having three different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and also harmonizing the US FDA labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries. Upon further discussion of the drug product name and strength between the Office of New Drugs (OND) and Office of Policy and Pharmaceutical Quality (OPPQ) teams, a consensus was reached that the drug product established name and strength should be expressed in terms of the salt (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling would include a statement stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole. For details regarding this decision, refer to the Memorandum filed in DARRTS on 3/21/24 by Jibril Abdus-Samad, OPQ/OPPQ/COSS.

L139: ## 3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
L140: The primary evidence of effectiveness and safety of ceftobiprole for the proposed indications of the treatment of SAB and ABSSSI in adults, and CABP in adult and pediatric patients were provided in five clinical trials. Four of the trials were submitted for efficacy evaluation of ceftobiprole. The HABP/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (VABP) trial was submitted to support the safety evaluation. All five studies were randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multicenter, phase 3 studies. The active control and the ceftobiprole dosing used in each study varied based on the clinical condition being treated. The endpoint evaluations in each trial were also adjusted based on the clinical indication. Additional data from post-marketing surveillance from other countries along with a review of literature publications were evaluated to support the safety evaluation. See Section 7.3 for further details.
L141: Key review issues that were identified during the review are addressed in greater detail in Sections 6.3 for efficacy and Section 7.7 for safety. Overall, the submitted clinical trials were adequate for the safety and efficacy evaluation of ceftobiprole. Table 5 provides an overview of the clinical trials relevant to the review of ceftobiprole's efficacy and safety.

L157: ## 5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical Pharmacology
L158: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L159: ## Nonclinical Ceftobiprole PK/PD Information
L160: Several studies were conducted to examine the nonclinical pharmacokinetics (PK)/pharmacodynamics (PD) of ceftobiprole in murine thigh and pneumonia models. Percent of time that free-drug concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (%ofT&gt;MIC) was best correlated with ceftobiprole efficacy, indicating that antibacterial activity of ceftobiprole is time dependent, similar to other beta-lactams (see Section 14.1.1 for more information).
L161: ## **Identification of PK/PD Target**
L162: An efficacy study was performed in neutropenic thigh-infected mice given single subcutaneous doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40, and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation was used to calculate the dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10 kill over 24 hours. The free time above MIC (fT &gt; MIC) values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from PK and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains and five strains of gram-negative bacteria, including *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae* and *P. aeruginosa* and *E. cloacae* (see Section 14.1.1 for more information). The results of fT &gt; MIC to achieve bacteriostasis, 1-log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 7.

18 L
Plasma protein binding	The protein binding of ceftobiprole is 16% and is independent of ceftobiprole concentration across the range of 0.5 to 100 µg/mL (Study FK5789 and Study FK6157).
Drug as substrate of transporters	Ceftobiprole is not a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp), breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2), BSEP, organic anion-transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1. Mass balance results	Elimination
A mass balance study for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was not submitted for review.
Clearance	5 L/hr
Half-life	The terminal half-life of ceftobiprole is approximately 3 hours, ranging from 2.4 to 4.11 hours across the phase 1 studies.
Metabolic pathway(s)	Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Ceftobiprole medocaril is the prodrug of the active form, ceftobiprole. Conversion from ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole occurs rapidly and is mediated by non-specific plasma esterases. Ceftobiprole undergoes minimal metabolism to an open-ring metabolite which is microbiologically inactive. Systemic exposure of the open-ring metabolite is approximately 4% of the parent exposure.
Primary excretion pathways (% dose)	The main route of elimination of ceftobiprole is by renal excretion, by glomerular filtration. Following single dose administration, approximately 89% of the administered dose is recovered in the urine as active ceftobiprole (83%), the open-ring metabolite (5%) and ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (<1%; Study CSI-1004).
Body weight	Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adults based on body weight. Dose adjustment is not needed.
L185: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L186: Characteristic	Drug Information
Age	No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adults based on age. Dose adjustment is not needed.
Renal impairment	Ceftobiprole AUC increase was 2.5-fold and 3.3-fold higher in adult subjects with moderate renal impairment (CL_{CR} 30 to < 50 mL/min), and 3.3-fold in severe renal impairment (CL_{CR} < 30 mL/min). Dose adjustment is recommended in moderate and severe renal impairment in adults and in pediatric patients > 2 years of age. No clinically significant difference in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adult patients with ESRD (CL_{CR} < 15 mL/min) compared to healthy adult subjects based on limited PK data and PK modeling and simulation. Ceftobiprole was demonstrated to be hemodialysable in patients receiving ceftobiprole
Hepatic impairment	The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of ceftobiprole was not evaluated. However, hepatic impairment is not expected to alter the elimination of ceftobiprole because ceftobiprole is mainly excreted by the kidneys. Dose adjustment is not needed.
Inhibition/induction of metabolism	Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as Perpetrator)
In vitro studies did not show a clinically relevant inhibitory or induction potential of ceftobiprole toward cytochrome P450 (CYP) 1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, or 3A4/5 (Studies 1009572, FK6366, and FK6604, FK5831/XT053012, FK6603/XT083004, and XT223040)
Inhibition/induction of transporter systems	In vitro studies suggest ceftobiprole is not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, or OCT2 (XT138008, XT228043).
Ceftobiprole inhibits OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 in vitro (Study XT138008).
Concomitant administration of ceftobiprole and substrates of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 is not recommended (see Section 8.2.1 and 14.1.5).
As ceftobiprole is not an inducer of CYP3A4 in vitro, no evaluation was done for P-gp induction.

L188: ## 6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
L189: ## 6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential Effectiveness
L190: The Applicant conducted probability of target attainment (PTA) analyses based on nonclinical PK/PD targets to support the adequacy of the proposed dose regimens including the renal function-based dose adjustments.
L191: Based on the observed PK and MIC data from the subjects evaluated in the phase 3 trials, the percentage of subjects who achieved the PK/PD targets associated with stasis and 1-log kill were determined.
L192: The Applicant's proposed dosages were evaluated in a single phase 3 trial for each respective indication (Table 10). The dosages used in the phase 3 clinical trials reflect the final
L193: recommended dosages. Dose adjustments are required for patients with renal impairment (See Section 8.1 for more information).

500 mg of ceftobiprole is equivalent to 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium
L197: These dosages were evaluated in target attainment analyses using simulated subjects by creatinine clearance (CL_{CR}) group and those resembling the clinical trial population on Day 1 (and Day 10 for the SAB indication). Target attainment was assessed based on median and randomly assigned free-drug plasma %fT&gt;MIC targets associated with net bacterial stasis and a 1-log10 CFU reduction from Baseline.
L198: Among simulated subjects with SAB, the percent probabilities of target attainment were &gt;99% for both stasis and 1-log10 CFU reduction over the MIC distributions on Day 1 and Day 10. For the ABSSSI and CABP indication, Day 1 target attainment rates differed slightly based on the bacterial species with &gt;99.9% for *S. aureus*, 100% for *Streptococcus* species, and ranged from 87.2 to 87.6% for *Enterobacteriales* in simulated subjects with ABSSSI and 100% for *S. pneumoniae*, &gt;99.9% for *S. aureus*, and ranged from 87.0 to 87.4% for *Enterobacteriales* in simulated subjects with CABP (see Section 14.5 for analysis results).
L199: ## **Dosage in Pediatric Patients with CABP**
L200: The recommended dosage in pediatric subjects with CABP is outlined in Table 11. Evidence of effectiveness for the proposed ceftobiprole dosage in CABP pediatric patients ages 3 months and older is based on safety and PK data in pediatric patients as well as extrapolation of effectiveness from adult CABP patients. Because CABP is pathophysiologically similar in adults and pediatric patients aged 3 months and older, the efficacious ceftobiprole exposures in adults are expected to also be effective in pediatric patients. Population PK analyses demonstrate that estimated ceftobiprole exposures resulting from the proposed dosage in pediatric CABP patients are similar to the efficacious exposures in adults, thus enabling extrapolation of effectiveness from adults to pediatric patients. Additionally, supportive evidence of effectiveness for the proposed dosage is provided by the results of probability of PK/PD target attainment analysis (see Section 14.5 for more information).

L207: ## 6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L208: ## 6.2.1. SAB, Trial BPR-CS-009
L209: ## 6.2.1.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-009
L210: Trial BPR-CS-009 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The trial protocol was reviewed as a special protocol assessment (SPA) under investigational new drug application (IND) 64407. This was a randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-arm, multi-center trial in adult hospitalized subjects with SAB, including infective endocarditis (IE), which was conducted in two parts. Part 1 enrolled an initial cohort of subjects (Cohort 1) for a maximum treatment duration of 28 days as animal studies had indicated the potential of an increased risk of convulsions with prolonged ceftobiprole treatment duration (&gt; 4 weeks) and no prior clinical studies of ceftobiprole with this treatment duration had been conducted. Based on a safety evaluation of Cohort 1, the Data and Safety Monitoring Board decided that it was safe to proceed to Part 2. Part 2 allowed a longer treatment duration of up to 42 days and the inclusion of subjects with more difficult to treat infections such as osteomyelitis and epidural or cerebral abscess who were excluded from Cohort 1. Subjects with left-sided infective endocarditis (LIE) diagnosed after randomization were also permitted to continue in the trial.
L211: Following a screening period of up to 72 hours, subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive intravenous (IV) ceftobiprole or daptomycin \pm aztreonam. The randomization was stratified by Trial site, dialysis status, and prior antibacterial treatment use within 7 days before randomization. Following the completion of treatment, visits were scheduled at end-of-treatment (EOT) (within 72 hours of the last Trial drug administration), Day 35 (\pm 3 days), Day 42 (\pm 3 days), and at post-treatment evaluation (PTE) on Day 70 (\pm 5 days) post-randomization. Note that the Day 35 and Day 42 visits could have been active treatment periods for subjects in Part 2
L212: requiring up to 42 days of treatment. The total duration of the Trial for each subject was approximately 10 weeks.
L213: A total of 390 subjects were planned to be randomized, and a total of 390 subjects were actually randomized and comprised the intent-to-treat (ITT) population (ceftobiprole n = 192; comparator n = 198). An independent blinded data review committee (DRC) comprising six infectious diseases experts was assembled to review detailed subject profiles, including imaging and microbiological and laboratory results, of all subjects in the ITT population, to assess the baseline categories of complicated SAB, the response outcome for the primary endpoint, and the secondary endpoints of microbiological outcomes and death attributed to SAB.
L214: ## **Primary Endpoint**
L215: Overall success assessed by the DRC at the PTE visit assessed in the modified intent-to-treat population.
L216: Overall success was defined as all of the following criteria being met:
L217: - Subject alive at Day 70 (\pm 5 days) post-randomization
- No new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection
- Resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms
- Two negative blood cultures for *S. aureus* (without any subsequent positive blood culture for *S. aureus*):At least one while the subject was on active study treatment; AND
- Confirmed by at least one subsequent negative blood culture for *S. aureus*Either in the period between 7 days after the EOT Visit and the PTE Visit
- Or at the PTE Visit
L218: Treatment failure was defined as any of the following:
L219: - Premature discontinuation of study treatment due to DRC assessed lack of efficacy or for adverse events (AEs) that represented manifestation of disease progression or relapse, at any time between first dose of study drug and the PTE visit.
- Development of new metastatic or other complications related to SAB between Day 8 and the PTE visit.
- SAB relapse/reinfection based on evidence from a blood culture positive for *S. aureus* (after documented clearance of *S. aureus* from the bloodstream and clinical improvement) between the EOT and PTE visits.
- Receipt of systemic non-study antibacterial treatment, other than those permitted under the protocol, for the treatment of SAB. This included subjects who were prematurely discontinued from study therapy due to an AE, but who required continuation of antibacterial treatment for SAB.
- Treatment of infections other than SAB with systemic non-study antibacterial treatment which was potentially effective against *S. aureus*, and which was considered by the DRC to
L220: have a relevant impact on the primary endpoint in accordance with guidelines provided in the protocol.

- Death for any reason between first administration of study drug and the PTE visit.
- Indeterminate outcome, defined as any data needed to determine whether the outcome was success or failure was missing at the PTE visit, including but not limited to:Missing PTE visit, or missing key data to evaluate the primary endpoint
- Lost-to-follow-up, or subjects who withdrew consent prior to the PTE visit
- Subjects not meeting the criteria for success or failure, or subjects not meeting all criteria for overall success
- Requirement for systemic antibacterial treatment for SAB beyond EOT.
L221: ## Secondary Endpoints
L222: - All-cause mortality assessed at Day 70 (PTE Visit) in the mITT population (ITT subjects who received any dose of study medication, and had a blood culture positive for *S. aureus* at Baseline).
- Microbiological eradication assessed by the DRC at Day 70 (PTE Visit) in the mITT population.
- The overall success rate in the ITT, mITT, and clinically evaluable (CE) populations:At the EOT and PTE (ITT and CE populations only) visits
- At the EOT and PTE visits, for RIE versus non-IE SAB
- At the EOT and PTE visits, by renal-function status
- Development of new metastatic foci or other complications of SAB after Day 7 were assessed in the mITT and CE populations.
- Time to *S. aureus* bloodstream clearance in the mITT and CE populations, defined as the elapsed time (days) from randomization to bloodstream clearance, with bloodstream clearance defined as the occurrence of two consecutive study days with blood-culture-negative assessments for *S. aureus*; bloodstream clearance in subjects with intermittent positive on treatment blood cultures started after the last positive blood culture. Subjects with *S. aureus* relapse or reinfection as per DRC assessment were not considered as bloodstream clearance.
- Safety and tolerability.
- Pharmacokinetics.
L223: ## **6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial BPR-CS-009**
L224: The trial enrolled adult subjects with complicated SAB, defined as subjects with at least one positive blood culture for *S. aureus* at Baseline, signs and symptoms of bacteremia (fever, white blood cell [WBC] count, tachycardia, and/or hypotension), and one of the following underlying conditions or complications: chronic intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis,
L225: persistent SAB, definitive native-valve RIE, ABSSSIs, or metastatic infections of native tissue (e.g., septic arthritis, septic/suppurative thrombophlebitis, visceral abscess, septic pulmonary emboli).
L226: Subjects with osteomyelitis or cerebral/epidural abscess were to be enrolled in Part 2 only.
L227: Subjects who received treatment with potentially effective anti-staphylococcal systemic antibacterial treatment for more than 48 hours within 7 days before randomization were excluded from the trial unless they met the criteria for persistent SAB.
L228: ## **Inclusion Criteria**
L229: Subjects meeting all of Inclusion Criteria 1 – 5 and at least one of Inclusion Criteria 6 – 11 were eligible for enrollment:
L230: - Male or female \ge 18 years of age.
- Informed consent signed by the subject (or by their legally acceptable representative, if appropriate) indicating that they understood the purpose of, and procedures required for, the trial and were willing to participate in the trial.
- SAB, based on at least one positive blood culture obtained within the 72 hours prior to randomization:Identified by culture laboratory report, or
- Positive diagnostic test for *S. aureus* (e.g., polymerase chain reaction [PCR], tube coagulase test and fluorescent in situ hybridization) obtained from a blood culture.
L231: At least one of the following signs or symptoms of bacteremia within the 72 hours prior to randomization (may be based on measurements obtained before or after informed consent but within the 72 hours prior to randomization):
L232: - Fever &gt;38^{\circ}\text{C} / 100.4^{\circ}\text{F} measured orally, &gt;38.5^{\circ}\text{C} / 101.3^{\circ}\text{F} measured tympanically, &gt;37.5^{\circ}\text{C} / 99.5^{\circ}\text{F} measured by axillary method, or &gt;39^{\circ}\text{C} / 102.2^{\circ}\text{F} measured rectally
- WBC count &gt;10.0 \times 10^9/\text{L} or &lt;4.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}, or &gt;10\% immature neutrophils (bands)
- Tachycardia (heart rate &gt;90 beats per minute [bpm])
- Hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] &lt;90 mm Hg)
- Required duration of study antibacterial treatment \le 42 days.
- SAB in subjects undergoing chronic intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
- Persistent SAB: documented failure of bloodstream clearance, defined as a positive blood culture for *S. aureus* within the 72 hours prior to randomization, after prior appropriate anti-staphylococcal treatment (except failure under daptomycin therapy) of at least 3 complete days.
- Other forms of complicated SAB, including the following:ABSSSIs
- Metastatic infection of native tissue. Examples include but were not limited to:
- Septic arthritis or bacterial joint infection/empyema
L233: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L234: - Septic or suppurative thrombophlebitis
- Visceral soft-tissue abscesses requiring \le 42 days of study antibacterial treatment
- Septic pulmonary emboli/infarction
- Definite native-valve RIE by Modified Duke's Criteria.
L235: ## Prohibited Concomitant Medications
L236: Concomitant systemic antibacterials that provide activity against *S. aureus* were prohibited during the period from randomization up to the PTE visit. The use of non-study antibacterial treatment during the trial was not necessarily considered to be an outcome of 'failure'. The significance of concomitant potentially effective non-study antibacterial treatment (except aztreonam, metronidazole, nitrofurantoin, and oral vancomycin) was assessed in accordance with the guidelines provided in the clinical study report (CSR) to determine whether the treatment had an impact on the primary endpoint.
L237: ## Permitted Antibacterial Treatments
L238: The following concomitant antibacterial medications were permitted:
L239: - In the daptomycin treatment arm, aztreonam using a standard-dose regimen at the site for coverage of gram-negative infections (i.e., for polymicrobial bloodstream infections, or gram-negative non-bloodstream infections). Subjects randomized to the ceftobiprole arm who were considered to require coverage against gram-negative infections received dummy treatment with placebo so that blinding was maintained during the active treatment phase.
- In both treatment arms:Nitrofurantoin for urinary tract infections
- Metronidazole using a standard-dose regimen at the site for coverage of anaerobic infections
- Oral vancomycin was considered a non-systemic antibiotic and was permitted for use at any time during the trial.
L240: ## 6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial BPR-CS-009
L241: ## Disposition of Subjects
L242: The disposition of subjects is described in Figure 1. A total of 390 subjects were randomized to receive either the ceftobiprole (n = 192) or daptomycin (n = 198) treatment. Three subjects did not receive study treatment (1 in ceftobiprole arm and 2 in the daptomycin arm). Two subjects, both in the ceftobiprole arm, were determined by central laboratory results not to have a confirmed positive blood culture for *S. aureus* at Baseline.

L251: ## Baseline demographic and disease characteristics
L252: As shown in **Table 13**, the baseline demographic and disease characteristics in the mITT population were generally balanced across the treatment arms. Subjects in the mITT were mostly White (96%), European (93%) or male (69%) with a median age of 58 years. Approximately 8% of subjects were Hispanic or Latino. Of note, 54% of subjects had a fever at baseline, 13% were on chronic dialysis and 40% had an abnormal WBC at baseline. Prior antibacterial medication use was common at 70% and concomitant (allowed) antibacterial medication use was also common using aztreonam (34%) or metronidazole (6%).

L270: ## **Analysis Sets**
L271: The analysis sets defined in the trial were as follows:
L272: ## **ITT Population**
L273: All randomized subjects.
L274: ## **The Safety Population**
L275: All randomized subjects who received at least one dose of study drug.
L276: ## **mITT Population**
L277: ITT subjects who received any dose of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive for *S. aureus* at baseline.
L278: ## **CE Population**
L279: Protocol-compliant ITT subjects who complied with important aspects of the study.
L280: ## **Sample Size Determination**
L281: The sample size estimate was based on:
L282: - A point estimate for overall success of 40% in each treatment arm in the mITT population
- One-sided alpha level of 0.025
- Power of &gt;80%
- Non-inferiority margin of 15% for the between-arm difference in the primary endpoint
L283: With these assumptions, enrollment of 175 subjects per treatment arm (total of 350 subjects) was required for the mITT population. Assuming that approximately 90% of subjects in the ITT population had confirmed SAB and therefore were to be included in the mITT population, it was necessary for 195 subjects per arm (total of 390 subjects) to be randomized and receive Trial treatment.
L284: ## **Statistical Methods**
L285: ## **Primary Analysis**
L286: The Trial was designed to determine whether ceftobiprole was non-inferior to daptomycin for the primary outcome measure of overall success at the PTE Visit at Day 70 (\pm 5 days) after randomization, in the mITT population. The specified NI margin was 15%.
L287: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L288: *This 15% NI margin was based on 7 studies from the pre-penicillin era reporting clinical outcome (survival) in untreated subjects with SAB which combined suggested all-cause mortality (ACM) of 76% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 71%, 79%) as well as 3 studies of mortality in SAB subjects receiving antibacterial treatment which suggested an ACM of 16% (95% CI: 12%, 20%). The MI is estimated to be 51% for ACM. The protocol stated that "An estimation of MI for an overall success endpoint is not possible, as this was not reported in the historical studies,*
L289: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L290: which considered survival to be success" but that "the mortality data suggest that M1 for a clinical/overall success outcome for SAB would similarly be very large, i.e., in the range of 50%, when outcomes are compared for untreated subjects and subjects who received effective antibacterial treatment." The NI margin of 15% was chosen based on clinical judgement. With a sample size of 250–350 subjects (in the mITT population), an NI margin of 15% would allow for the determination of noninferiority only if the point estimate between ceftobiprole and daptomycin is &lt;5%.
L291: The difference in the percentage of responders (i.e., subjects with overall success at PTE) (ceftobiprole arm minus the comparator arm) was determined, and a two-sided 95% CI for the difference was computed, with adjustment for actual dialysis status, and prior antibacterial treatment use (defined as receipt of medications within 7 days prior to randomization that were categorized as potentially effective systemic antibacterial treatments). Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) weights were used for the stratum weight in the calculation of the CI. The non-inferiority hypothesis test was a one-sided hypothesis test performed at the 2.5% level of significance. If the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the difference in response rates in the mITT population was greater than -15%, the noninferiority of ceftobiprole to daptomycin therapy was concluded.
L292: ## Secondary Analyses
L293: Secondary analyses considered the above approach for overall success assessed by the DRC at the EOT visit in the ITT and CE populations. All-cause mortality was assessed in the mITT and ITT populations and time to death was calculated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Survival rates (event-free probability estimates) at Day 28 and Day 70 in the ITT and mITT populations were provided and associated two-sided 95% CIs were calculated using the Greenwood formula. The hazard ratio for all-cause mortality and associated 95% CI were provided using a Cox proportional-hazard model, with treatment and actual stratum (dialysis status and prior antibacterial treatment use) as covariates. *S. aureus* clearance was analyzed in a similar manner as all-cause mortality.
L294: ## 6.2.1.4. Results of Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-009
L295: ## Primary and Key Secondary Endpoint Analyses
L296: Table 15 shows the results from the primary analysis and reasons for failure. For the primary endpoint of overall success at the PTE visit at Day 70 (\pm 5 days) after randomization in the mITT population, noninferiority was demonstrated with an adjusted difference (Ceftobiprole – Daptomycin) of 2.0% with a lower 95% confidence limit of -7.1% which exceeded the pre-specified NI margin of -15%. Similar findings were observed when considering the primary endpoint in the CE population.
L297: Reasons for failure were generally similar between the treatment arms; however, there was a lower proportion of failures due to 'Requirement for systemic antibacterial treatment for SAB beyond protocol-defined maximum study treatment duration' in the ceftobiprole arm, 9/57 (15.2%) vs. 15/62 (24.2%). A slightly lower proportion of failures due to SAB relapse/reinfection was also observed in the ceftobiprole arm, 2/57 (3.5%) vs. 4/62 (6.5%). The most common reason for treatment failure in both treatment arms was 'Treatment of SAB with systemic non-study antibacterial treatment, other than those permitted under the protocol' which
L298: was more common in the ceftobiprole arm accounting for 20/57 (39.1%) versus 19/61 (30.6%) of failures.

L311: ## **Subgroup Analyses**
L312: Subgroup analyses for the primary endpoint, 'overall success based on DRC assessment at the PTE visit' by gender, race and ethnicity are shown in Table 17. Treatment differences tended to be more favorable in ceftobiprole subjects among subjects who were 18-34 years, male, White and Hispanic/Latino. There were a few other notable findings. Among subjects 18 to 34 years of age, overall success rates were 17/20 (85%) versus 11/19 (57.9%) which showed a nominally significant treatment difference of 26.7% (95 CI: 0.4, 53.0) favoring ceftobiprole. Also, among non-White subjects, overall success rates were 0/5 (0%) for subjects in the ceftobiprole arm versus 5/6 (66.7%) for subjects in the daptomycin arm which showed a nominally significant treatment difference of -55.6% (95 CI: -100.0, -10.5) favoring daptomycin.
L313: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L314: *The small number of non-White subjects combined with the nominally significant difference in non-White subjects favoring daptomycin may make generalizing trial results to non-White subjects more difficult. Of note, this difference was likely due to the small sample size and random variation since the subjects' reasons for failure were often not directly related to a lack of treatment effect.*

The adjusted between-arm difference was -8.3% (95% CI: -26.3, 8.6) in favor of daptomycin.

L355: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L356: was defined as the conditional probability that if the DRC or the Investigator makes an assessment of overall success (or failure) then the other (i.e., the Investigator or the DRC) will also make an assessment of overall success (or failure). There was 98.0% agreement between the DRC and investigator assessments for overall success, and 95.2% agreement for failure.

L360: 267 of the 277 assessments of overall success by the Investigator were also rated as overall success by the DRC, and 267 of the 268 assessments of overall success by the DRC were also rated as overall success by the Investigator. Concordance for overall success was calculated as the total number of agreements in overall success ratings between the Investigator and the DRC (n = 534, 267 + 267) divided by the total number of overall success ratings by either the Investigator or the DRC (N = 545, 277 + 268), resulting in a concordance of overall success of 98.0% (534/545).
L361: 109 of the 110 assessments of failure by the Investigator were also rated as failures by the DRC, and 109 of the 119 assessments of failure by the DRC were also rated as failure by the Investigator. Concordance for failure was calculated as the total number of agreements in failure between the Investigator and the DRC (n = 218, 109 + 109) divided by the total number of failures rated by either the investigator or the DRC (N = 229, 110 + 119), resulting in a concordance of failure of 95.2% (218/229).

L369: ## Conclusions
L370: Trial BPR-CS-009 met its primary objective of demonstrating noninferiority for the pre-specified primary endpoint of overall success based on DRC Assessment at the PTE (Day 70) Visit. Key secondary endpoints also appeared to be generally consistent with noninferiority. Overall, there were no major concerns regarding the evidence of effectiveness.
L371: Minor concerns are related to subject selection with approximately 96% of subjects being 'White,' which may limit the generalizability of efficacy findings to other races. There were also less favorable treatment differences in a few subgroups receiving ceftobiprole ('non-White'),
L372: ‘U.S.’, ‘MRSA’ and ‘polymicrobial BSIs’), although sample sizes tended to be small. Findings of large regional differences in clinical overall success rates at PTE (e.g., Ukrainian vs. Ex-Ukrainian sites) may also limit generalizability. Although the high success rates at the Ukrainian sites did not positively affect the estimated treatment difference in this trial, they could affect the assumptions used in the justification of the NI margin (see 6.3 for more details).
L373: ## 6.2.2. ABSSSI, Trial BPR-CS-008
L374: ## 6.2.2.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-008
L375: Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The protocol was reviewed as a SPA under IND 64407. The design of pivotal trial BPR-CS-008 was based on the current FDA Guidance for Industry Acute Bacterial Skin and Skin Structure Infections: Developing Drugs for Treatment, October 2013, including with respect to the efficacy endpoints, timing of assessments, and statistical considerations.
L376: This was a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, parallel-arm, multicenter trial in adult hospitalized subjects to establish the safety and efficacy of ceftobiprole compared with vancomycin plus aztreonam in the treatment of ABSSSIs. The trial had a noninferiority design, with vancomycin plus aztreonam selected as an established comparator regimen. Vancomycin, recognized in current guidelines as the standard treatment for ABSSSI, is effective against gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA. Aztreonam was added to vancomycin due to its efficacy against gram-negative bacteria.
L377: Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted in three phases:
L378: - Pre-treatment: Screening and baseline, duration up to 24 hours.
- Active treatment: Randomization and at least 5 days, and up to 10 days, of study drug administration. Study treatment could be extended up to 14 days if required.
- Post-treatment: An EOT visit within 24 hours after last treatment, a test-of-cure (TOC) visit 15 – 22 days after randomization and at least 5 days after EOT, and a last follow-up visit 28 – 35 days after last treatment. In addition, survival status (Alive; Dead; Lost to Follow-up) was to be verified for evaluation of all-cause mortality. Survival status (by telephone or visit) was to be obtained at Day 28 (\pm 2 days).
L379: The total duration of the study for each subject was approximately 5 – 7 weeks.
L380: The selected ceftobiprole dose was the dose approved for the HABP and CABP indications in non-U.S. countries: 500 mg administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 8 hours, to be adjusted for subjects with moderate or severe renal impairment (500 mg of ceftobiprole is equivalent to 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium). The dose of vancomycin was 1,000 mg or 15 mg/kg administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 12 hours; this could be modified for renal function. The dose of aztreonam was 1,000 mg per 0.5-hour IV infusion every 12 hours, to be adjusted for subjects with severe renal impairment; the need for treatment with aztreonam was to be reassessed at the 72-hour study Visit.
L381: ## Other design considerations:
L382: - Primary measurement of the target lesion size was to be performed using a flexible ruler, measuring longest length, and maximum width perpendicular to the length.
- Measurements were to be performed at Screening (prior to randomization and within the 6 hours prior to first dose of study drug), twice on Day 2, Day 3, and Day 4, and once on Day 8, and the EOT, TOC, and last follow-up visits. On days when two measurements were obtained, the measurements were to be taken at least 8 hours apart. Infection-site assessment includes incision/drainage, erythema, heat/localized warmth, pain/tenderness to palpation, fluctuance, and swelling/induration.
- A digital photograph was to be obtained at Screening, at the early clinical response assessment (48–72 hours after first treatment), and at the EOT and TOC Visit, for each subject (primary ABSSSI lesion), and was to be used for documentation purposes and as source data. Digital photography was not to be used for the measurement of the ABSSSI lesion size area; the determination of the ABSSSI lesion size area was to be solely based on the ruler measurements.
- Clinical success was to be assessed by the investigator using a four-point scale relative to the baseline assessment: cured, improved, stable, or worsened. In case of worsened (e.g., bacteremia, osteomyelitis, amputation), signs and symptoms needed to be documented as AEs.
- Concomitant antibacterial therapies, other drug therapies, and non-drug procedures were to be assessed at all scheduled study visits.
- Survival status (by telephone or visit) was to be obtained at Day 28.
L383: The primary objective for Trial BPR-CS-008 was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to early clinical response based on percent reduction in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours after first treatment in the ITT population.
L384: The main secondary objective was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization in the ITT and Clinically Evaluable populations.
L385: ## **Primary Endpoint**
L386: Early clinical response based on percent reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours after first study-drug administration, measured in subjects who did not receive rescue therapy, and were alive. A clinical response was defined as a percentage reduction in lesion size greater than or equal to 20 percent compared to baseline.
L387: ## **The Main Secondary Endpoint**
L388: Investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization, and at least 5 days after the EOT, assessed in the ITT and CE populations.
L389: ## 6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial BPR-CS-008
L390: The eligible subject population for trial BPR-CS-008 included adults who were diagnosed with ABSSSI (cellulitis/erysipelas, major cutaneous abscess, wound infection) with regional or systemic signs of infection, who were hospitalized (in a hospital or equivalent medical confinement or clinical research unit) and required IV antibacterial treatment. Subjects with other forms of ABSSSI or uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections were excluded, as were those with infections related to prosthetic devices, or infections which required more than two surgical interventions.
L391: Subjects who had received any systemic antibacterial treatment within 14 days, or topical antibacterial on the primary lesion within 96 hours, before first infusion of study drug, were also excluded.
L392: The minimum lesion size had to be 75 cm2 using standardized measurements (longest length of the lesion by widest width perpendicular to that length) with a flexible plastic ruler. The proportion of subjects with major cutaneous abscesses was also not to exceed 30% of the total subject population included.
L393: ## Inclusion Criteria
L394: Subjects meeting all of the following:
L395: - Male or female, aged \ge18 years.
- Diagnosis of ABSSSI, meeting at least one of the definitions in (a) to (c) below. Local symptoms must have started within the 7 days prior to the Screening visit.
- Cellulitis/erysipelas, defined as a diffuse skin infection characterized by all of the following within 24 h:Rapidly spreading areas of erythema, edema, and/or induration with a minimum total lesion surface area of 75 cm2.
- No collection of pus apparent upon visual examination.
- At least two of the following local signs of infection:erythema
- induration
- localized warmth
- pain or tenderness on palpation
- swelling/edema
L396: 4. Major cutaneous abscess, defined as infection characterized by a collection of pus within the dermis or deeper that is apparent upon visual examination before or after therapeutic intervention and is accompanied by all of the following within 24 h:

- Erythema, edema and/or induration with a minimum total lesion surface area of 75 cm2.
- At least two of the following local signs of infection:fluctuance
- incision and drainage required
- purulent or seropurulent drainage
- localized warmth
- pain or tenderness on palpation
14. Wound infection, defined as infection of any apparent break in the skin characterized by at least one of the following:

- Superficial incision/surgical site infection meeting all the following criteria:involves only the skin or subcutaneous tissue around the incision (does not involve fascia).
- occurs within 30 days of procedure.
- purulent drainage (spontaneous or therapeutic) with surrounding erythema, edema and/or induration with a minimum total lesion surface area of 75 cm2.
- Post-traumatic wound (including penetrating trauma, e.g., needle, nail, knife, insect and spider bites) meeting the following criterion within 24 h:Purulent drainage (spontaneous or therapeutic) with surrounding erythema, edema and/or induration with a minimum total lesion surface area of 75 cm2.
15. At least one of the following regional or systemic signs of infection at the Screening visit:

- Lymph node tenderness and volume increase, or palpable lymph node proximal to the primary ABSSSI.
- Fever \ge 38^{\circ}\text{C}/100.4^{\circ}\text{F} (regardless of method of measurement).
- WBC count &gt;10.0 \times 10^9/\text{L} or &lt;4.0 \times 10^9/\text{L}.
- &gt;10\% immature neutrophils (band forms).
16. Requirement for IV antibacterial treatment.

17. Willing and able to adhere to study procedures (including prohibitions and restrictions) as specified in this protocol.

18. Willing and able to remain hospitalized (in a hospital or equivalent medical confinement or clinical research unit) until completion of the early-clinical-response assessment for the primary endpoint.

19. Informed consent signed by the subject, or their legally acceptable representative if appropriate, indicating that they understand the purpose of, and procedures required for, the trial, and are willing to participate.

L398: ## Prohibited Concomitant Medications
L399: Concomitant systemic antibacterial drugs were prohibited during the trial up to the TOC visit, with the following exceptions:
L400: - Vancomycin PO 125 mg or 250 mg every 6 hours, fidaxomicin PO 200 mg q12h, or metronidazole IV or PO 500 mg q8h, in both treatment arms, for the treatment of *Clostridium difficile* infections.
- Metronidazole IV as adjunctive therapy in both treatment arms for coverage of anaerobic bacteria.
- Nitrofurantoin at any time during the trial in both treatment arms as it does not achieve therapeutic blood levels.
L401: All NSAIDs were prohibited until 72 hours after start of treatment, and were then permitted only after early clinical response had been determined.
L402: The administration of steroids (&gt;40 mg per day prednisolone, or equivalent), or immunosuppressants was prohibited between administration of first study drug and the TOC Visit.
L403: Chronic systemic therapy with calcineurin-inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, or cyclosporin), mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolate sodium, azathioprine, sirolimus, and topical antibacterial drugs on the primary lesion was prohibited from randomization to the TOC Visit.
L404: ## Non-Drug Adjunctive Therapy
L405: Adjuvant surgical treatment was recognized as appropriate and necessary for adequate treatment of wound infections and abscesses. Subjects were evaluated at Screening to determine whether more than one intra-operative surgical intervention was required. Those expected to require more than two surgical interventions in the operating room for the ABSSSI were to be excluded from the trial.
L406: When indicated, the initial surgical procedure was to be performed before randomization, and subsequent procedures performed no later than 48 hours after the start of treatment.
L407: Adjunctive therapies permitted for the treatment of ABSSSI at any time were debridement at the bedside, topical solutions, including antiseptic agents such as povidone-iodine (topical solutions did not contain anti-microbial agents), and local bedside wound care in accordance with hospital protocols.
