L1604: ## Conclusion
L1605: Despite the increased deaths in the VABP subgroup who received ceftobiprole compared to those who received linezolid/ceftazidime, most of the deaths do not appear to be related to the study treatment itself. The increased deaths in the VABP subgroup may have been due to chance, as there was a small number of subjects in the VABP subgroup relative to the entire trial. In addition, the acuity and severity of illness in this subgroup may have led to increased deaths overall, thereby confounding the association between deaths and trial treatment. However, information on increased mortality in VABP subjects treated with ceftobiprole will be included in the ceftobiprole labeling as a warning, emphasizing that ceftobiprole is not approved for the treatment of VABP.
L1606: ## 7.7.2. Imbalance in Adverse Events Related to Thrombosis in Trial BPR-CS-009
L1607: ## Issue
L1608: An increased frequency of thrombosis was observed in the ceftobiprole arm as compared to daptomycin arm in the BPR-CS-009 trial. This was evaluated further as a key safety issue due to nonclinical signals of thromboembolic events discussed in Section 7.1 and summarized below.
L1609: ## Background
L1610: In the nonclinical/toxicology studies, there were findings of thrombi observed across species (at the injection site in the rat, marmoset, and dog) and emboli noted in marmosets in the heart, lung, kidney, mostly with administration of ceftobiprole for a duration of over 1 month. The Applicant stated that in the 13-week studies in rats and marmosets, the thrombus formation was around the tip of the infusion catheter. When examining the histological changes, it was consistent with mechanical irritation by the infusion catheter, subsequently causing vascular-wall irritation and subsequent thrombus formation. The mechanical irritation was attributed to the small size of the veins relative to the large size of the implanted catheter. Ultimately, it was thought that the thrombus formation was caused by local irritation and injury along with the higher concentrations of ceftobiprole as compared with the clinical studies.
L1611: ## Assessment
L1612: When grouping the PTs using the narrow FMQ, there was a slightly higher incidence of thrombosis in the ceftobiprole vs. the comparator arm.

L1621: A grouped query for thrombosis was created encompassing the following PTs: thrombosis, DVT, atrial thrombosis, venous thrombosis limb, portal vein thrombosis, splenic infarction, and
L1622: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L1623: arteriovenous fistula thrombosis. As myocardial infarction is often due to a different pathophysiology, PTs related to myocardial infarction/acute myocardial infarction were not included in the grouped query. In addition, the PT 'thrombophlebitis' (for subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) was combined in another grouped query termed 'phlebitis' given similar pathophysiology; the description of the AE is noted in Table 110 below. Using the thrombosis grouped query, there was still an imbalance with the ceftobiprole group experiencing 7 (3.5%) cases of thrombosis compared to 2 (1%) in the daptomycin arm. Of note, all AEs in the thrombosis grouped query in both treatment arms were considered 'not related' to trial drug by the investigator. The AEs in the daptomycin arm included splenic infarction and DVT; the DVT was an SAE and occurred 9 days after the last dose of daptomycin.
L1624: To obtain more information about the context of the thrombosis events, an information request was sent to the Applicant on November 2, 2023. The Applicant's response as well as subject narratives and profiles were evaluated to determine if there was any definitive relationship between ceftobiprole and thrombi formation (i.e., the formation of a thrombus in the presence of ceftobiprole without alternative cause). The 7 subjects with the grouped query of thrombosis are described below. None led to death or treatment discontinuations, and two were SAEs ([REDACTED](b) (6)).
L1625: Another information request was sent to the Applicant on February 23, 2024, requesting further clarification for subjects with AEs of DVT, venous thrombosis limb, thrombosis and thrombophlebitis who had a history of thrombotic events prior to enrollment in the trial, and that information is included in Table 1 as well as in the narratives below.
L1626: - [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 58-year-old female with a medical history of recently diagnosed DVT, osteomyelitis and epidural abscess in T8-9, abscess drainage eight days prior to enrollment and spinal decompression six days prior enrollment, who had a reported AE of thrombosis on Day 11. The verbatim term was post-thrombotic disease of the lower extremities and in the information request response, the Applicant clarified that the subject was diagnosed with DVT 6 days prior to starting ceftobiprole and experienced a mild post-thrombotic syndrome of the lower extremities on Day 11. The Applicant stated that these events were clearly linked as the post-thrombotic syndrome (i.e., the chronic condition) was seen as favorable progress of the pre-study deep vein thrombosis (i.e., the acute condition).
- [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 65-year-old female with a medical history of thrombophlebitis (diagnosed 46 days prior to enrollment), aortic arteriosclerosis, and hypertension who had a reported AE of DVT on Day 15. During the same time as the thrombophlebitis, the subject also had a chronic wound on the right calf for which she had a necrectomy two days prior to enrollment. The exact location of the initial acute thrombophlebitis on the right lower extremity was not recorded, and the location of the DVT was at the right medial gastrocnemius. The Applicant noted that it is possible that the exact location could have been different and the two events were distinct, however, the chronic wound and necrectomy may have predisposed for the development of a DVT. Additional risk factors for thrombosis included not receiving DVT prophylaxis and the presence of an immobilization bandage. Immobilization is a known risk factor for DVT (Samama 2000).
- [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 45-year-old female with a medical history of hemodialysis, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, nontunneled central venous catheter placement 12 days prior to enrollment who had an SAE of atrial thrombosis on Day 5 which was found on transesophageal echocardiography. She was placed on heparin and a repeat echocardiography
L1627: showed reduced size of the thrombosis while she was still on ceftobiprole treatment. It is unlikely that ceftobiprole contributed to the formation of atrial thrombosis as the thrombosis improved during treatment.
L1628: - [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 48-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes mellitus, multiple surgeries two months prior to enrollment (pancreatectomy 64 days prior, colectomy 62 days prior, splenectomy 3 days prior), who had an AE of venous thrombosis limb on Day 8. The verbatim term was right leg phlebothrombosis and the Applicant noted that the subject had been diagnosed with a right lower extremity DVT 21 days prior to starting ceftobiprole. The Applicant also noted that it is unclear whether the pre-study DVT and the AE of venous thrombosis limb occurred at the exact same location and it is uncertain whether these were related events.

- [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 34-year-old female with a medical history of intravenous drug abuse who had an AE of venous thrombosis limb and a reported term of right basilic vein thrombosis on Day 13. Prior to the AE, she had not been receiving any DVT prophylaxis, had a peripherally inserted central catheter placed in the right basilic vein on Day 3 which was removed once the DVT was diagnosed, and had a history of intravenous drug abuse which are all associated with a risk of thrombi formation (McColl et al. 2001). The association with ceftobiprole is unlikely, but not fully excluded.

- [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 45-year-old male with a medical history of chronic pancreatitis, distal pancreatectomy 11 days prior to enrollment, who had an AE of portal vein thrombosis on Day 8. In a study involving 991 subjects who underwent distal pancreatectomy, 2.1% were diagnosed with portal vein thrombosis (Kamath et al. 2014). As portal vein thrombosis is a very specific type of thrombosis and may have been due to prior surgery, it is less likely that there was an association with ceftobiprole.

- [REDACTED](b) (6) is a 58-year-old female with a medical history of arteriovenous fistula, hemodialysis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus experienced an SAE of arteriovenous fistula thrombosis on Day 45 which was 23 days after ceftobiprole was discontinued. Because of the prolonged time between the onset of the thrombosis and the last dose of ceftobiprole, an association between the thrombosis and ceftobiprole is unlikely.
L1629: ## Conclusion
L1630: Out of the 7 subjects discussed above, 4 had events that appeared to be unrelated to ceftobiprole (one had pre-existing DVT and post-thrombotic syndrome, one had portal vein thrombosis in the setting of pancreatic surgery, and 2 had no clear temporal association with ceftobiprole). However, in 2 subjects, it was not clear if the DVT or venous thrombosis was the same as the episode occurring several days before treatment with ceftobiprole [REDACTED](b) (6). Another subject had an upper extremity DVT in the setting of a peripherally inserted central catheter line [REDACTED](b) (6). The remaining 3 subjects in the ceftobiprole arm who experienced venous thrombosis had other risk factors for venous thrombosis such as immobilization, multiple surgeries, or IV lines, however, the contribution of ceftobiprole could not be fully excluded. Given the nonclinical findings of thromboemboli in multiple animal species, a similar finding in humans may be possible, but overall less likely given confounding factors in the study population (e.g., multiple comorbidities, prolonged hospitalization, prior surgical procedures, and inconsistent DVT prophylaxis).
L1631: NDA 218275
L1632: ## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L1633: Notably, no significant imbalance in thrombosis events was noted in the other clinical trials discussed in this review. Additionally, thromboembolic disease has not been reported with ceftobiprole in the post market setting (from countries where it is approved for indications of HABP and CABP). However, ceftobiprole will be administered to subjects with SAB who may be prone to valvular insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, and potentially prolonged hospitalization predisposing them to venous thrombosis. Therefore, thrombosis will be included in section 6 of the labeling under the subsection "Selected Adverse Reactions of ZEVTERA in Adult Patients" occurring at a rate &lt; 2\% in the clinical trials and will be further monitored by routine surveillance in the post-market setting.

L1639: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L1640: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L1641: ## 8.1.1. Renal Impairment
L1642: Renal impairment had a significant effect on ceftobiprole exposure. Following a single infusion of ceftobiprole 250 mg over 30 minutes, systemic exposure (area under the concentration-time curve [AUC]last) was 29% higher in subjects with mild renal impairment, and 2.5-fold, and 3.3-fold higher in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively, compared to subjects with normal renal function. Urinary recovery was approximately 74% to 32% in subjects with mild to severe renal impairment, respectively (see Section 14.2.3). Dose adjustment for renal impairment is recommended as depicted in Table 111 based on 1) FDA analyses and PK simulations 2) the Applicant's population PK analyses 3) evaluation of target attainment rates for the proposed doses in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment and 4) safety and efficacy data from the pivotal phase 3 efficacy trials using the proposed dose adjustments.

L1656: ## 8.1.2. End-Stage Renal Disease and Patients Receiving Intermittent Hemodialysis
L1657: Dosage in subjects with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) (defined as a CrCL &lt; 15 mL/min) and subjects receiving intermittent hemodialysis (iHD) is supported by simulated ceftobiprole exposures derived using a population PK model fit with data from nine phase 1 studies and three phase 3 studies, including 20 subjects with SAB who received ceftobiprole after iHD (see Section 14.5.2.3). These simulations, in combination with adequate target attainment, support a ceftobiprole dosage of 250 mg every 24 hours in subjects with CrCL &lt;15 mL/min and subjects receiving iHD, when dosed after the iHD session (see Section 14.5.2.3). The Applicant conducted a PK study in subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis, where six ESRD subjects requiring hemodialysis were matched by age and weight with six healthy subjects. The PK of ceftobiprole was compared between healthy subjects and ESRD subjects dosed after dialysis (post-dialysis) or dosed before dialysis (pre-dialysis). In ESRD subjects receiving a 4-hour dialysis session after a 2-hour 250 mg ceftobiprole intravenous infusion, 28% of the dose was removed by hemodialysis.
L1658: The clinical pharmacology reviewer noted that plasma data used for PK analysis by the Applicant was not consistent with the raw data provided in the assay report. Specifically, the plasma concentrations at 30 min for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, ceftobiprole, and the opening metabolite from all the ESRD subjects during the period 2 (i.e., postdialysis) of the study were switched with their respective concentrations at 90 min in the Applicant's report.
L1659: Upon further analysis the reviewer also noted questionable concentration-time profiles for four out of six ESRD subjects when dosed after hemodialysis. As illustrated in Figure 17, ceftobiprole concentrations approximately ten-fold higher than expected were observed in Subjects [REDACTED] (b) (6) during the infusion phase. Furthermore, the plasma concentration time profiles were considered abnormal for Subjects [REDACTED] (b) (6) as well due to unexpected additional peaks after the infusion was over. Taken together, the questionable data in 4 out of the 6 ESRD subjects studied precluded reliable estimation on ceftobiprole PK characteristics in the ESRD subjects dosed after hemodialysis.

Taken together, the proposed dosage of 250 mg IV q24h for ESRD subjects is acceptable given the similar steady state exposures compared to subjects with normal renal function, high rates of target attainment on Day 1 and similar efficacy noted in the phase 3 SAB Trial.

L1717: ## 8.1.5. Hepatic Impairment
L1718: The effects of hepatic impairment on the PK of ceftobiprole have not been evaluated. Ceftobiprole does not undergo significant hepatic metabolism and has low plasma protein binding. As such, hepatic impairment is not expected to alter the elimination of ceftobiprole. Dosage adjustments are not necessary in patients with impaired hepatic function.
L1719: ## 8.1.6. Body Weight
L1720: A single-dose study was conducted to investigate the PK of ceftobiprole in subjects with morbid obesity in comparison to non-obese subjects. Exposure to ceftobiprole was lower in morbidly obese subjects attributed to a larger volume of distribution and a higher CL, resulting in ~17% lower exposure which is unlikely to be clinically relevant. No doses adjustment based on body weight were made in the phase 3 studies.
L1721: The effect of weight was also evaluated in the adult population PK (PopPK) analysis and in the PK/PD target attainment analysis. Although body weight was a statistically significant predictor of interindividual variability in CL, central and peripheral volumes of distribution in the PopPK analysis, ceftobiprole dose adjustments based on body weight are not required to ensure sufficient PK/PD target attainment.
L1722: ## 8.1.7. Gender
L1723: The effects of gender on ceftobiprole PK were evaluated in two phase 1 studies, as a primary objective of study BAP00036 and a secondary objective of Study CSI-1004. Systemic exposure to ceftobiprole was higher in females, with 21% higher C_{max} and 15% higher AUC_{last} in BAP00036 and 24% higher C_{max} and 14% higher AUC_{0-inf} in CSI-1004, compared to males. The higher systemic exposure in females observed in these studies was attributed to a lower body weight in females.
L1724: The effect of gender was also evaluated in the PopPK analysis. In the adult PopPK model, gender identified as statistically significant predictor of the interindividual variability observed in the peripheral volume of distribution but was not found to be clinically relevant. Dose adjustment is not indicated based on gender.
L1725: ## 8.1.8. Other Intrinsic Factors
L1726: The effects of adult age and race were evaluated in the PopPK analysis and were not identified as statistically significant covariates. Accordingly, dose adjustments based on age or race are not indicated.
L1727: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L1728: ## 8.2.1. Pharmacokinetics Based Drug-Drug Interactions
L1729: ## Ceftobiprole as a Victim of Drug-Drug Interactions
L1730: In hepatocytes, ceftobiprole was slowly metabolized to the open-ring hydrolysis product BAL1029 and does not appear to undergo significant hepatic metabolism.
L1731: In vitro studies showed that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp), breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2), bile salt export pump, organic anion-transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1 in vitro. Ceftobiprole was a substrate of the renal uptake transporters organic anion transporter 1 (OAT1) and organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) but not OAT3 in vitro. Ceftobiprole was not evaluated as a substrate of multidrug and toxin extrusion protein 1 (MATE1), or MATE2-K as active secretion does not contribute to ceftobiprole elimination.
L1732: ## Ceftobiprole as a Perpetrator of Drug-Drug Interactions
L1733: In vitro studies showed that ceftobiprole did not inhibit or induce cytochrome P450 (CYP) 1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, or 3A4/5 at therapeutic plasma concentrations. Hence, ceftobiprole is unlikely to result in clinically relevant CYP-mediated DDIs.
L1734: In vitro studies showed ceftobiprole was an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 but was not an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, or OCT2.
L1735: The in vitro transporter inhibition assessment based on calculated R values is outlined in Table 118. A drug has the potential to inhibit a transporter in vivo if the R value is &gt;1.1. Since the in vitro studies indicate that a drug is an OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 inhibitor, we recommend the Applicant conduct an in vivo drug interaction study evaluating ceftobiprole as an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATB1B3 transporters as a post-marketing requirement (see Section 14.1.5).

L1752: ## 8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of Reproductive Potential
L1753: ## Nonclinical Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology and Lactation Data
L1754: Intravenous administration of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to pregnant rats and monkeys during organogenesis showed no evidence of adverse fetal developmental outcomes at doses approximately 1.4 times and 0.9 times the MRHD, respectively, based on BSA comparison. Intravenous administration of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to rats 2-weeks prior to mating, during organogenesis, and through lactation resulted in no significant adverse fertility or fetal development effects in offspring at doses approximately 1.4 times the MRHD, based on BSA comparison. Slight reductions in number of pups born per litter and decreased postnatal survival up to day 4 after birth were associated with maternal toxicity (mortality, reduced food consumption and body weight gain in surviving females during gestation). No offspring adverse effects were observed in surviving pups during the postnatal postweaning development period (Days 5 through 22) at doses up to 360 mg/kg.
L1755: Pregnant rats were administered ceftobiprole at doses of 175, 250, and 360 mg/kg/day from 14-days pre-mating through lactation/postpartum day 21. Ceftobiprole was excreted in rat milk at levels of approximately 20% of the corresponding maternal plasma ceftobiprole levels. The concentration of ceftobiprole in animal milk does not necessarily predict the concentration of drug in human milk.
L1756: ## 9. Product Quality
L1757: Approval With a Postmarketing Commitment
L1758: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L1759: The Office of Pharmaceutical Quality (OPQ) review team assessed NDA 218275 with respect to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC). The proposed drug product, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, is a sterile lyophilized powder filled into single-dose glass vials, which need to be reconstituted and further diluted for intravenous infusion. Each drug product vial contains 667 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole) and is supplied in a carton containing 10 single-dose vials. The majority of CMC information provided in the NDA to assure and demonstrate the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the proposed drug product, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, was found to be adequate. However, since the proposed drug product is an injectable powder for reconstitution, it needs to comply with applicable guidances and regulations to ensure that the excess solid in a vial is sufficient to allow for withdrawal and administration of the net container content of the drug product. Therefore, additional finished drug product and in-process controls are needed. In addition, the currently established drug product assay and impurity limits are considered acceptable on an interim basis and should be reassessed based on the stability testing results for three new drug product batches manufactured using a revised drug substance assay calculation. These issues will be addressed through two PMC studies (the PMC descriptions and draft timelines are included in Section 24, below). All manufacturing and testing facilities were found acceptable. An exception to the FDA/USP salt policy guidance was made for the drug name, strength and equivalency statement in consultation with OND.

L1823: ## **Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, Pharmacokinetics**
L1824: The absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of ceftobiprole medocaril (BAL5788) and ceftobiprole (active metabolite, BAL9141) was investigated in multiple species. Pharmacokinetics were assessed in the mouse, rat, rabbit, cynomolgus monkey, marmoset and dog. Excretion was primarily investigated in the rat.
L1825: ## **Absorption**
L1826: Nearly all studies have been conducted via the intravenous route, except for juvenile toxicology study conducted in rats by the subcutaneous route.
L1827: ## **Distribution**
L1828: Low-to-moderate plasma protein binding (18 to 40%) was detected in mouse, rabbit, dog, monkey, and human plasma, across a concentration range of 30-300\muM. A comparative study of mouse and human showed that protein binding in both species is low.
L1829: In a rat exploratory quantitative whole body autoradiography study following a single intravenous administration of ^{14}C radiolabeled ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (20 mg/kg), quantifiable levels of radioactivity (&gt;0.29 mcg-equiv/g) were detected in all tissues with a low overall distribution into most organs and tissues. The highest concentrations of radioactivity 15 minutes post-dose were found in the kidney (34.2 and 32.3 mcg-equiv/g in the cortex and medulla, respectively), skin (19.63 mcg-equiv/g), tooth pulp (19.17), liver (18.96 mcg-equiv/g), lung (17.3 mcg-equiv/g), blood (17.04 mcg-equiv/g), connective tissue (15.73 mcg-equiv/g), aorta (11.61 mcg-equiv/g) and stomach mucosa (11.98 mcg-equiv/g). Lower levels (below 10 mcg-equiv/g) were detected in mandibular and mesenteric lymph nodes, adrenal gland, thyroid, adrenal gland, pituitary gland, salivary glands, lacrimal gland, harderian gland, pineal body and muscle with lowest levels detected in the brain and spinal cord (0.38 and 0.58 mcg-equiv/g, respectively). Elimination of radioactivity was rapid (declining over 10-fold in 7 hours) except for the kidney with an estimated half-life of over 24 hours. Elimination of radioactivity was predominantly by the renal route (82% of the dose within 48 hours). In a similar distribution study in mice, the highest concentrations of radioactivity across tissues were found in the coagulating gland (78.29 mcg-equiv./g), the excretory organs kidney (30.43 and 24.24 mcg-equiv./g in cortex and medulla, respectively) and liver (26.26 mcg-equiv./g), as well as in skin and aorta. Elimination from tissues was rapid (declining concentrations by 10fold in 2 hours) with detectable levels only in the kidney cortex and liver by 24 hours.
L1830: ## Metabolism
L1831: The parent pro-drug compound BAL5788 is rapidly metabolized to BAL9141. BAL9141 is further metabolized to the open lactam ring form (BAL2070, up to 10% of the urinary compounds in this form). Further metabolism of BAL9141 into open ring forms were seen in multiple species (up to 4 other metabolites, ~5%).
L1832: The metabolism of BAL5788 (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium) was investigated in vitro using primary cultures of hepatocytes from livers of humans, rats, mouse, dog, marmoset, and cynomolgus monkeys and rat and mouse brain homogenates and rat liver and kidney homogenates. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug) was rapidly metabolized to Ro 63-9141, which in turn metabolized to the open beta-lactam ring form, BAL 65-2070. The percentage of metabolism at 48 hours is shown below.

L1836: - In an Applicant report (BAP00069), the comparative metabolism of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was investigated in vivo after administration of a single dose of radiolabeled (^{14}\text{C}) ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (13.3 mg/kg). The report included the metabolic profiles in rat plasma, urine, bile and kidney, rat brain and marmoset urine. The majority of the drug was shown to be eliminated in the urine. Within 5 to 10 minutes, the majority of the drug was converted from ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug to ceftobiprole). Approximately 10% of the compound detected in urine was the open ring form (Ro 65-2070) with other 4 metabolites detected (below 5%). Small amounts of ceftobiprole were detected in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of rats (1 to 2%). There did not appear to be significant differences in the metabolic profiles of males and females.

L1842: ## Excretion
L1843: Urinary excretion accounted for the majority of BAL5788 elimination in all species. Excretion was primarily investigated in the rat with 95% of the dose administered recovered in the urine after four days post dose. Cumulative excretion in rat showed 73% eliminated in the urine, 17% in the feces, 3% in the cage wash and 1% left in the carcass.

L1847: ## Interactions
L1848: In vitro studies ceftobiprole (active metabolite) did not appear to be a substrate or cause inhibition of several human proteins that may have a role in drug-drug interactions including human efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein, BCRP, bile salt export pump [BSEP] and MRP2) or human uptake transporters (organic anion-transporting polypeptide [OATP]1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, OCT2, OAT1 and OAT3).

L1862: For reference, the following compound identifiers have been used for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug): BAL5788-001, BAL0005788-001, BAL5788, JNJ-30982081, JNJ-30982081-(b) (4), Ro 65-5788, Ro 65-5788/001 and for its active metabolite ceftobiprole (Ro 63-9141/000, 63-9141, BAL9141)
L1863: ## BAP00230. A Two-Week Toxicity Study of BAL5788 (Prodrug of BAL9141) Via Intravenous Infusion in Dogs Followed by a Two-Week Recovery Period
L1864: ## Key Study Findings
L1865: - Histaminergic reaction (reddening of the skin, face edema, injection of the oral mucosa, vomiting and salivation) primarily associated with the shorter infusion time (30 minutes). Findings significantly decreased with a longer infusion time for the high and medium dosed animals (2 hours). These findings correlated with a dose dependent increase in plasma levels of histamine that returned to control levels after infusion (approximately 4 hours from start of infusion).
- Injection site hemorrhage (slight) of the subcutis observed in all animals, hyperplasia of the tunica intima was observed at 50 and 100 mg/kg/day in males and females.
- No observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) considered at 100 mg/kg/day (1.2-fold the MHRD based on body surface area [BSA] comparisons).
L1866: **Table 128. Study Information**
L1867: Study Features and Methods	Details
GLP Compliance:	Yes
Dose and frequency of dosing:	0, 25, 50 and 100 mg/kg/day (calculated as BAL9141)
Route of administration:	IV infusion (over 30-minute period, initially, changed to 2 hours due to severe toxicity at the mid and high dose groups) once daily
Formulation/vehicle:	BAL5788 (batch PO103)/ 5% dextrose
Species/strain:	Dog/ Beagle
Number/sex/group:	2-3/sex/group
Age:	5-7 months (males: 7.2-10 kg; females: 7.1-9.3 kg)
Satellite groups/unique design:	Infusion time changed from 30 minutes to 2 hours for the 50 and 100 mg/kg groups
Deviation from study protocol affecting interpretation of results:	None that had an impact on the outcome of the study.

## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L1871: **Table 129. Observations and Results**
L1872: Parameters	Major Findings
Mortality	No unscheduled deaths
Clinical signs	
In nearly all treated animals: On first day of dosing (Day 0) vomiting, reddening of the auricles, conjunctiva, oral mucosa were observed for approximately 30 minutes after the end of infusion. In 4/5 males and 3/5 females, facial edema, reddening of the skin (i.e., extremities) or erythema were observed over the whole-body during infusion. Sedation, scratching, prone or sitting position, spontaneous defecation, decreased activity, somnolence, vomiting, and or retching and salivation were also observed in some animals during infusion. After extension of the infusion time to 2 hours, the incidence of vomiting was reduced (about 3/5 males and females vomited during infusion), reddening of auricles was still observed in some animals but the reddening of the conjunctiva and oral mucosa were no longer observed. Although occasional vomiting and reddening of the auricles and conjunctiva were observed, incidence and severity of findings decreased over time.

Body weights	No treatment-related changes
Ophthalmoscopy	No treatment-related changes
Hematology	No treatment-related changes
Clinical chemistry	
Histamine levels evaluated in 25 and 100 mg/kg/day groups on days 0 and 1 were slightly elevated (~ 2-fold) in one animal at 25 mg/kg at 0.5 hours after start of infusion (back to control levels within an hour) and greatly elevated in all animals at 100 mg/kg/day (up to 160-fold) at 0.25 and 0.5 hours after start of infusion (back to control levels at approximately 4 hours). This correlated with observations of reddening of the skin and facial edema (primarily at the high dose).

Urinalysis	No treatment related changes
Gross pathology	Red foci at the site of injection observed across all groups, including controls
Organ weights	No treatment-related changes
Histopathology	Slight kidney eosinophilic droplets in the proximal tubules of the kidney at 50 mg/kg/day (1-2/3 males and females) and in all animals at the 100 mg/kg/day (persistent at the end of the recovery period).
Adequate battery: Yes	Injection site hemorrhage (slight) of the subcutis observed in all animals, hyperplasia of the tunica intima was observed at 50 and 100 mg/kg/day in males and females.

L1935: - Urine levels of BAL5788 and BAL9141 were evaluated on days 0 and 13 [high dose only], at 0-2, 2-4, 4-6 h after the start of infusion. The urinary levels of BAL5788 were highly variable and ranged from 0-277 mcg/mL. Levels of BAL9141 were slightly less variable and showed some dose dependence. On Study Day 0, the highest measured urinary concentrations of BAL9141 were 15170 mcg/ml (male, 360 mg/kg, 0-2h) and 17280 mcg/ml (female, 250 mg/kg, 4-6 h). On day 13, the highest urinary concentration of BAL9141 was 23160 mcg/mL (male, 360 mg/kg, 4-6 h). On day 27, the highest urinary concentrations of BAL9141 were 15070 mcg/mL (male, 175 mg/kg, 2-4h) and 16330 mcg/mL (female, 360 mg/kg, 4-6 h). There was no indication of drug precipitation in the distal tubules or collecting tubules.

L1953: ## **TOX-7154/ A Thirteen-Week Toxicity Study of BAL5788 (Prodrug of BAL9141) Via Intravenous Infusion in Common Marmosets Followed by a Four-Week Recovery Period**
L1954: ## **Key Study Findings**
L1955: - Mortality was observed at all doses tested (\ge 50 mg/kg). The cause of death was attributed to thrombosis/emboli in the lung and heart, potentially originating from the injection site thrombi.
- Clinical signs in early death animals included clonic/tonic seizures, decreased activity, vomit and hind leg paralysis. Lymphoid depletion and atrophy were observed in the spleen, thymus and lymph nodes.
- Liver findings (only in males) included hepatocellular vacuolization and hypertrophy.
- Lung findings included fibrosis and thrombosis.
- No NOAEL was established in this study due to mortality observed at all doses tested.

The Applicant attributed these changes to stress. The cause of death was likely due to thrombo-embolic events in 5/6 males and all of the females.

L1969: ## BAP00728. A Thirteen-Week Toxicity Study of BAL5788 (Prodrug of BAL9141) Via Intravenous Infusion in Rats Followed by a Four-Week Recovery Period
L1970: ## Key Study Findings
L1971: - Mortality observed in males \ge 250 mg/kg/day. Prior to death/euthanasia, no unusual signs (6/11 males) or decreased activity, emaciation, hypothermia and/or clonic/ tonic convulsions (5/11 males) were observed.
- Primary findings of surviving animals were thrombi and necrosis at the injection site which was more prevalent and severe in treated animals compared to controls. Kidney findings included eosinophilic tubules and the presence of foreign material in the tubules/ducts, likely due to drug precipitate.
- NOAEL was considered at 125 mg/kg/day (equivalent to 0.5-fold the maximum human dose of 2.84 g/day based on body surface area comparisons).

L2004: ## Local Tolerance
L2005: ## **TOX7588. A Local Irritation Study of BAL5788 by Intravenous Injection to Rabbits**
L2006: ## Methods
L2007: The purpose of this study was to test the irritation potential of 2 ceftobiprole medocaril sodium formulations made from slightly different synthesis routes (BAL5788 A, intended for dilution in saline and B intended for dilution in 5% dextrose). BAL5788-A (drug product [DP] formula, batch # 30-4EXP, 91.6% purity); BAL-5788-B (New DP formula, batch # I050605, 100.9% purity) in 5 % dextrose was administered by IV injection to male Kbt rabbits (2.9-3.4 kg, 15 weeks old, 3/group) into the ear vein (0.05 mL/site/day) once daily for 8 consecutive days. Positive control bromosulfalein (BSP) diluted into saline. Clinical signs (daily), body weight (prior to administration), observations of the injection site, and histopathology of the injection site (Day 8) were conducted/observed.
L2008: ## Results
L2009: There were no clinical signs. Body weights did not change significantly from controls. At 10 mg/mL very slight to slight inflammation was observed in most rabbits (including controls) around the injection site between Days 3 and 5. Positive control rabbits showed slight or moderate inflammation along with thrombi throughout the dosing period. With the exception of the positive control animals where cell infiltration, desquamation edema, fibrosis, hemorrhage and thrombus were noted, there were no noteworthy findings. There were no significant differences in local irritation between the BAL5788 formulations A and B; BAL5788 was no more irritating than normal saline this 8- day study in rabbits.
L2010: ## **TOX7904. A Local Irritation Study of BAL5788 by Intravenous Injection to Rabbits-2**
L2011: ## Methods
L2012: BAL-5788-B (formula, batch # I050605, 100.9% purity), vehicle (5% dextrose) or positive control BSP were administered intravenously into the ear vein at 0, 2 and 10 mg/mL either as fresh solution or aged for 30-hour period to male Kbt:JW rabbits (2.9-3.3 kg, 16 weeks old, 3/group) for 8 consecutive days.
L2013: Clinical signs (daily), body weight (prior to administration), observations of the injection site, and histopathology of the injection site (Day 8) were conducted/observed.
L2014: ## Results
L2015: There were no abnormal clinical signs or changes in body weight. There were no dose dependent changes in inflammation as compared to physiological saline at the injection site. The BSP animals showed slight to moderate inflammation and small thrombi. No significant differences in microscopic observations were made with BAL5788 or physiological saline. The positive controls showed cell infiltration, desquamation edema, fibrosis, hemorrhage and thrombi. Aging BAL5788 did not result in greater local irritation potential.
L2016: ## 13.1.2.2. Genetic Toxicology
L2017: For reference, the following compound identifiers have been used for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug): BAL5788-001, BAL0005788-001, BAL5788, JNJ-30982081, JNJ-30982081-(b) (4), Ro 65-5788, Ro 65-5788/001 and for its active metabolite ceftobiprole (Ro 63-9141/000, 63-9141, BAL9141)

L2151: ## **TOX8611. Ceftobiprole Medocaril Sodium (BAL5788): A Subcutaneous Toxicity Study in Neonatal and Juvenile Albino Rats**
L2152: ## **Key Study Findings**
L2153: - Mortality observed at the high dose (animals showed decreased or increased activity, pallor, vocalization and convulsions)

L2160: **Table 179. Observations and Results, TOX8611. Ceftobiprole Medocaril Sodium (BAL5788)**
L2161: Parameters	Major Findings
Mortality	A total of 15 pups were found dead or euthanized during the pre-weaning dosing period. One control group female was found dead on day 3 post-partum. At 50 mg/kg/day, 3 female pups were found dead (days 3, 13 and 2 post-partum). Another female in the 50 mg/kg/day group was subject to unscheduled euthanasia due to severe decreased health (abnormal gait, dehydration, decreased activity, lack of coordination, tremors, limited use of hindlegs). At 250 mg/kg/day 6 male pups and 2 female pups were found dead between days 2 and 15 post-partum. Clinical signs included thinness, skin pallor and empty stomach. One moribund male showed skin pallor, increased activity, decreased respiratory rate, increased vocalization and convulsions on day post-partum 3. There were no significant necropsy findings.
Clinical signs	At 250 mg/kg/day, post dosing (days 14-17) increased (5/50 males, 4/50 females) or decreased activity (5/50 males, 4/60 females), biting (3/50 males, 3/50 females), hypersensitivity, muscle tone increased (5/50 males, 3/50 females), post-dosing lack of coordination (6/50 males and females) and increased vocalization (8/50 males, 5/50 females). Findings were no longer observed 18 days post-partum. Red skin around the injection site observed mostly in the 250 mg/kg/day male and female pups at 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours and 4 hours post dosing for the first 3 days of dosing.
Body weights	Measured on all animals daily from Days 1 to 7 post-partum and on Days 10, 14, 18 and 21 post-partum. At 250 mg/kg/day, decreased weight gains compared to controls were observed in males (up to -12% by day 10 post-partum, slightly recovered at -8% by day 21 post-partum) and females (up to -13% by day 14 post-partum, slightly recovered at -8% by day 21 post-partum). At recovery, female weights were similar to controls, male weights remained slightly lower than controls (-3%).
Physical development	Crown to rump measurements: Measured post-cull day 1 and days post-partum 3, 7, 14 and 21. During pre-weaning crown-to-rump length was lower than controls (-3 to -5%) between days 21-24 post-partum at 250 mg/kg/day, consistent with lower body weights.
Physical development: Preputial separation days for group litters were slightly delayed at 100 and 250 mg/kg/day compared to concurrent controls (42.2 days for control and 44.2 and 44.4 days for treated males). However, group litter mean development values for treated males were comparable to the historical control range (41.5 to 44.7 days). There were no differences in mean day development of vaginal opening in treated females compared to controls.
Bone measurements: BAL5788-related consisted of a statistically significant decreased length of the tibia and femur in males at 250 mg/kg/day and decreased femur length of males at 100 mg/kg/day that were not observed at recovery.
Feed consumption	Feed consumption was decreased in 250 mg/kg/day males (-3%) and females (-8%) between post-partum days 21-24.
Ophthalmoscopy	No test article related findings
Hematology	No test article related findings

L2177: ## 13.1.2.5. Other Toxicology
L2178: ## 13.1.2.5.1. Other Studies
L2179: ## TOX 7589. An Antigenicity Study of BAL5788 in Guinea Pigs
L2180: ## Methods
L2181: For passive sensitization, male Hartley guinea pigs were injected subcutaneously (6 sites on the dorsal skin of 2 animals) with serum from the actively sensitized animals, then 4 hours later challenged with 25, 50 or 100 mg/kg of intravenously administered BAL5788 and Evan's blue dye. The dorsal skin was then examined for dye leakage. Actively sensitized animals were challenged with 100 mg/kg BAL5788 (pro-drug) and the reactions observed. Intravenous sensitization was evaluated at 1) 10 mg/kg/ BAL5788 (5 times week for 3 weeks, 2) 50 mg/kg/ BAL 5788 (5 times a week for 1 week) and 20 mg/kg (5 times week for 2 weeks, 3) 10 or 50 mg/kg, emulsified with Freund's complete adjuvant (FCA) or Freund's incomplete adjuvant (FIA) once weekly for 3 weeks. Positive control was 1 mg/kg subcutaneous ovalbumin emulsified with FCA once weekly for 3 weeks. The negative control was 5% dextrose IV or subcutaneous with FCA or FIA once weekly for 3 weeks. A 100 mg/kg challenge dose of BAL5788 (batch 30-4EXP, 93.8% purity) was used.
L2182: ## Results
L2183: One animal in the 50 mg/kg intravenous sensitization group died at day 4. No significant changes were noted in body weight. No abnormalities were seen in the sensitization with 5% dextrose or 10 mg/kg BAL with or without FCA/FIA. In the 50/20 mg/kg BAL alone groups, scratching and piloerection were observed in 1/5 guinea pigs (ASA grade 1). In the 50 mg/kg group with FCA/FIA, anxiety, tremor, piloerection, dyskinesia, dyspnea were seen in all animals within 60 minutes of challenge and 1/5 animals died (ASA reaction scores were 1/5 at 1, 2/5 at 2, 1/5 at 3 and 4). In the positive control group, one animal died within 6 minutes of challenge (ASA 4) while the remaining 4 animals had an ASA reaction grade of 2. No reactions were noted in the BAL5788 passively challenged animals. The positive control had 5/5 animals positive. BAL5788 was shown to have moderate antigenic potential.
L2184: ## Report 10016. Ro 63-9141/001: Phototoxicity Study (In Vitro)
L2185: ## Methods
L2186: The potential phototoxic potential of Ro 63-9141/001 (ceftobiprole, batch # 18116B2, 370-4500 mcg/mL) was evaluated an in vitro assay with Balb/c 3T3 mouse fibroblasts by incubating the test article in the cell culture system with or without exposure to a non-cytotoxic dose of ultraviolet light (ultraviolet A [UVA] wavelength of 240-4500 nanometers) or kept in the dark. Cytotoxicity was expressed as a dose dependent reduction of the growth rate of cells as determined by uptake of the vital dye Neutral Red one day after treatment. Negative control was the vehicle, PBS/ 3% dimethyl sulfoxide [DMSO]) and chlorpromazine was used as positive control.
L2187: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L2188: ## Results
L2189: There were no changes in cell viability at any concentration of drug tested or changes after exposure to UVA radiation as compared to cultures kept in the dark. Chlorpromazine, the positive control for UVA, behaved as expected (with a Dark/UVA discrimination factor for cytotoxicity of 66-fold). The study was valid and the test article was considered negative for phototoxicity.
L2190: ## Report 1004008. Ro 65-5788/001: In Vitro Assessment of Hemolysis, Plasma Turbidity and Plasma Precipitation in Dog Blood
L2191: ## Methods
L2192: The potential of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (13.3% or 133.3 mg/mL pro-drug, batch# 90402B2171202) to induce hemolysis and plasma turbidity was evaluated in vitro using venous dog blood. Vehicles used were saline and 5% glucose. Hemolysis was measured by spectrophotometer (hemoglobin %) and turbidity was evaluated visually.
L2193: ## Results
L2194: No significant hemolysis or plasma turbidity or precipitation were seen in dog blood under in vitro conditions in a 13.33% test solution of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium pro-drug (corresponding to 10% or 100 mg/ml of the active drug Ro 63-9141/000) at concentrations corresponding to 1.25% (12.5 mg/ml pro-drug). At higher concentrations, hemolysis of up to 7.3% and moderate to marked plasma turbidity and precipitation were observed.
L2195: ## Tox7587. Haemocompatibility Test with Human, Rat, and Marmoset Blood
L2196: ## Methods
L2197: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was evaluated at 5 concentration levels (1, 5, 12.5, 25 and 50 mg/mL) for hemocompatibility with rat, marmoset, and human blood at a volume ratio of 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 (1:5, 2:5 and 4:5) test material:blood. Reportedly, in the human, this ratio corresponds to administration of 1.6, 3.2 and 6.4 mL/min intravenous infusion rates. Hemoglobin release was determined following a 3-minute incubation at 37°C. For the plasma compatibility evaluation rat, marmoset, and human plasma were mixed with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium solutions at a ratio of 0.8 (4:5) test material:plasma. Samples were observed for flocculation, precipitation, and coagulation after 0.16, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 30 and 60 minutes at room temperature.
L2198: ## Results
L2199: No test article related hemolysis was observed at any dose tested in rat, marmoset. or human blood. When ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was mixed with human, rat, or marmoset plasma at a ratio of 0.8 (equivalent to an infusion rate of 6.4 mL/minute), dose dependent adverse reactions were observed (flocculation, precipitation, and coagulation) with increasing ceftobiprole medocaril sodium concentrations and increasing time. In all three species the adverse reactions (primarily precipitation) were observed \ge 2.5 mg/mL concentration level. At \ge 25 and with increasing time periods, flocculation and coagulation were also observed.

L2207: In a leachables assessment from samples stored both upright and in inverted position under both long-term (5 \pm 3 °C, for 0, 6, 12, 24 and 48 months) and accelerated storage (25 \pm 2 °C, 60% RH \pm 5\%, for 0, 3 and 6 months), three leachables ((b) (4))
L2208: were identified &gt; 5 mcg/day. A
L2209: comprehensive toxicological assessment was not provided by the Applicant (only an ECHA dossier was cited), however, reviewer assessments and derived PDEs are included below for (b) (4). The unknown leachable was reportedly measured below the 5 mcg/day threshold level (considered for both general toxicity and sensitization) under normal conditions for real time storage.

L2218: ## Other
L2219: Non-sensitizing to skin of guinea pig (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development Test Guideline 406)
L2220: Permitted Daily Exposure (PDE): The \text{ppm} NOAEC, corresponding to \text{mg/m}^3, from the 24-month inhalation study in rat was used to derive a PDE:
L2221: \begin{aligned}\text{NOAEL} &amp;= \text{NOAEC}(\text{mg/m}^3) \times \frac{6\text{hr}}{24\text{hr}} \times \frac{5 \text{ days}}{7 \text{ days}} \times \frac{\text{Respiratory volume of rat (L/day)}}{\text{Rat body weight (kg)}} \times \frac{1\text{m}^3}{1000\text{L}} \\ \text{NOAEL} &amp;= \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{m}^3} \times \frac{6\text{hr}}{24\text{hr}} \times \frac{5 \text{ days}}{7 \text{ days}} \times \frac{1\text{m}^3}{1000\text{L}} = \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg} \cdot \text{day}}\end{aligned}
L2222: Applying modifying factors of 5 for the extrapolation of rat data to human, 10 for variability between individuals, 1 for study duration, 1 for severity of toxicity studies, 1 for availability of a NOAEL and 10 for bioavailability. (The reported mean inhalation absorption of \text{in rat is } \text{%}).
L2223: This results in a PDE of \text{mg/day} of \text{in parenteral route:}
L2224: \text{PDE} = \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{kg}} \times 50 \text{ kg} \times \frac{1}{5 \times 10 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 10} = \text{mg/day}

L2241: ## 13.1.2.5.3. Safety of Impurities
L2242: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection (pro-drug (BAL5788) for ceftobiprole, BAL9141) will be given as an intravenous infusion and will be marketed as a sterile lyophilized powder for reconstitution (inactive ingredients are citric acid monohydrate in sodium hydroxide). There are no pharmacology/toxicology concerns for the excipients. The unit dose is 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium per vial (equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole). The MRHD is 2.67 g/day (equivalent to 2.0 g ceftobiprole). The animal data supports safety of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for up to 1 month duration, however, based on clinical data treatments for up to six weeks were permitted. We deferred to the clinical review team on the safety of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium administered for this extended duration.
L2243: The genotoxicity profile of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was mixed including a negative Ames assay, a positive mouse lymphoma assay, a negative forward mutation assay, and positive chromosomal assays for both the pro-drug and active metabolite suggesting clastogenic potential. However, in vivo ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was negative in both the micronucleus assay and rat liver unscheduled DNA synthesis reducing concern for potential clastogenic activity.
L2244: In considering potential and actual impurities in the drug substance (DS) and DP, the Applicant assessed genotoxic potential of several impurities using Derek quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) analysis (a second tool was not expected since initial phase 3 clinical trials were conducted prior to the publication of the ICH M7 Guidance). Expert analysis based on available scientific literature or data from studies conducted by the Applicant and purging assessments were also considered. In general, the Applicant followed ICH M7, particularly in assigning a classification of mutagenic potential to the impurities. The Applicant considered 155 compounds, classified 94 of them as class 4 or 5 (can be treated as nonmutagenic), and used purging calculations or direct analytical methods to demonstrate absence of 57 compounds. There were 5 impurities classified in classes 1, 2 or 3 and these were amongst the compounds demonstrated to be absent in the drug substance. The Applicant also provided a rationale for levels of (b) (4) guided by ICH Q3C Guidance, with special consideration of the short-term use of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection. For limit setting of impurities based on manufacturing experience and commercial process capabilities, the Applicant proposed the use of alternative thresholds higher than ICH Q3A and Q3B Guidance, including a reporting threshold of (b) (4), and qualification thresholds of (b) (4) for the drug substance (DS) and (b) (4) for the DP. These higher thresholds were jointly considered acceptable by CMC and pharm/tox teams (see CMC's separate reviews of DS and DP in Panorama). The impurities identification threshold for DS and DP was considered at (b) (4), as per ICH Guidelines Q3A/B. Data was also used from toxicology studies to set impurity thresholds for the drug product over the control of its shelf life.
L2245: A review of select impurities including impurities evaluated for their genotoxic potential in vitro and/or in vivo or for potential qualification based on nonclinical toxicology studies (primarily for those that exceeded the accepted DS and DP impurities thresholds) follows.
L2246: ## **Review of the Qualification of Impurities Based on Toxicological Studies**
L2247: The Applicant evaluated the potential qualification of impurities detected in the DP based on toxicological studies conducted with several batches of formulations used for nonclinical studies for a duration of up to 4-weeks in rats, marmosets, and dogs. Calculations of qualification limits were based on the study NOAELs from the respective nonclinical studies (selecting those with higher levels of individual impurities) and comparison to the levels in the clinical formulations at the MRHD. A total daily dose of 2.67 grams of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, equivalent to 2 grams of the active metabolite (ceftobiprole) was considered. Toxicological qualification levels considered in the calculations were (b) (4) in the DS and (b) (4) in the DP. The Applicant's calculations and assumptions were revisited and re-calculated by the reviewer using a similar approach to that used by the Applicant but including the application of a scaling allometric factor to determine a Human Equivalent Dose (HED) in the extrapolation of the individual impurities exposures to animals compared to humans. Tables 182 and 183 below, for the DS and DP (those not identified in the DP), show the list of impurities of concern (those found not to be fully qualified in toxicological studies), margins of exposure to the maximum recommended human dose and the individual impurities qualification status. In addition of impurity specifications for the DP, In Use specifications were considered for calculations when available.

L2256: ## **Conclusion of the Review of Impurities not Fully Qualified in Toxicology Studies**
L2257: The impurity qualification review indicates that the select individual impurities in the DS and DP are not adequately qualified based on the toxicology studies considered. However, the levels of these impurities in ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for the intended clinical treatment durations and indications are considered acceptable based on the following considerations: 1) The impurities specified below share significant structural similarities with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and represent a small fraction of the DP, therefore, these individual impurities are not likely to cause greater toxicities than those observed with exposure to the DP. 2) The overall analysis of the mutagenic potential of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (prodrug), which shares similar structural alerts with the individual impurities evaluated, indicates that ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and associated impurities are not likely to have mutagenic potential. 3) Although mixed results have been observed with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole in *in vitro* mutagenicity tests (negative in a limited Ames test, positive in the mouse lymphoma assay, but negative in a more recent HPRT forward mutation assay), primarily associated with the presence of [REDACTED] (b) (4) further *in silico* QSAR analysis based on application of expert knowledge and comparison to the most structurally similar analogs indicate that both compounds are predicted to be negative for bacterial mutagenicity. The analysis performed by FDA's Computational Toxicology Consultation Service experts included three QSAR state of the art models: Derek Nexus six 6.3.0 (DX), Leadscope Model Applier 2022.0.2.3 Bacterial Mut V2 model (LMA) model and CASE Ultra 1.9.0.8 GT1_BMUT model 1.9.0.2 (CU) and was consistent with ICH M2(R7) Guideline (i.e., prediction of bacterial mutagenicity using multiple complementary methodologies).
L2258: Although there are limitations in the qualification of impurities based on toxicological studies, the levels of impurities in ceftobiprole medocaril sodium are considered acceptable and no further evaluations of impurities for safety is warranted.

L2319: ## 14.1.1. Preclinical Studies to Determine the PK/PD Target of Ceftobiprole
L2320: ## Identification of PK/PD Index
L2321: The percentage of time during a dosing interval when the unbound drug concentration exceeds the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT&gt;MIC) has been identified as the PK/PD index that best correlates with the bactericidal activity of most \beta-lactam drugs.
L2322: Dose fractionation studies conducted with *S. aureus* American type culture collection (ATCC) 33591 confirmed the PK/PD index best correlated with in vivo efficacy was %fT &gt; MIC (Figure 23).
L2323: **Figure 23. Correlation of Ceftobiprole PK-PD Indices With Efficacy Against *Staphylococcus aureus* ATCC 33591.**
L2324: Source: Craig WA, Andes DR. In vivo pharmacodynamics of ceftobiprole against multiple bacterial pathogens in murine thigh and lung infection models. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2008 Oct;52(10):3492-6.

L2327: ## **Identification of PK/PD Target**
L2328: The activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in a mouse neutropenic thigh-infection model. Mice were given single subcutaneous doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40, and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation was used to calculate the dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10 kill over 24 hours. The %fT &gt; MIC values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from PK and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains (n = 8 *S. aureus* and n = 6 *S. pneumoniae*) and five strains of gram-negative bacteria, including *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, *P. aeruginosa*, and *E. cloacae*. The results of %fT &gt; MIC to achieve net bacterial stasis, 1-log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 197.
L2329: Since free-drug plasma %fT&gt;MIC targets from this study were only reported for net bacterial stasis and a 2-log10 colony forming unit (CFU) reduction from baseline, free-drug plasma %fT&gt;MIC targets associated with a 1-log10 CFU reduction from baseline were linearly interpolated by averaging the targets for net bacterial stasis and a 2-log10 CFU reduction from Baseline.
L2330: Overall, these pharmacodynamics studies suggested that bactericidal (1-log kill) %fT&gt;MIC values of approximately 30% and 50% would provide efficacious dosing for ceftobiprole for treatment of infections caused by gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, respectively.

L2338: ## **PK/PD Target in Acute Pneumonia Model**
L2339: Additional PK/PD studies in the neutropenic mouse lung infection model demonstrated that antibacterial effects were induced with %fT&gt;MIC values at 15 – 25% of the dosing interval for *S. pneumoniae* and *S. aureus*, including MRSA.
L2340: In the first study, neutropenic mice were infected with four strains of *S. pneumoniae* (including one penicillin-sensitive strain, one penicillin-resistant strain and two highly penicillin-, ceftriaxone- and cefotaxime-resistant strains) and administered either ceftobiprole or ceftriaxone. For the four tested strains of *S. pneumoniae*, the %fT&gt;MIC as a percent of the dosing interval ranged from 9 to 18% for ceftobiprole. This study evaluated total-drug, rather than free-drug, time over MIC.

L2368: ## 14.1.2. Protein Binding
L2369: Initial studies investigated the plasma protein binding of ceftobiprole by ultrafiltration in mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, marmoset, Cynomolgus monkey, and human (BAP00112, BAP00566). Results from both studies indicated that plasma protein binding was low, ranging from approximately 10% to 45% across species, and independent of drug concentrations (10 or 100 µg/mL). In humans, plasma protein binding ranged from 22.1% to 40.8%. These initial studies used a small sample size and showed a high intra- and inter-experimental variability for human plasma protein binding.

L2377: A second study (FK6157) was conducted to confirm the extent of plasma protein binding observed, due to differences noted in the later study versus the preliminary studies. Results again indicated that plasma protein binding was low and concentration independent, with a mean percent binding of 15.4%.

L2386: ## 14.1.3. Metabolism
L2387: Conversion of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole is very rapid in human plasma (38 seconds; study BAP00072). Inhibition studies with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid suggested that type A plasma esterases are involved in the cleavage of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole (study BAP00207). A mechanistic study investigating the enzymes involved in the hydrolysis of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium demonstrated a lack of specificity of this conversion which occurred both enzymatically (by paraoxonases and other hydrolytic enzymes) and non-enzymatically (Study FK6700).
L2388: In vitro hepatocyte studies indicated the primary metabolite is the open-ring hydrolysis product (study BAP00070). The prodrug ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is rapidly hydrolyzed, in contrast to the active moiety ceftobiprole, which is slowly metabolized. At least three additional, unidentified metabolites were present in trace amounts. Thus, ceftobiprole does not appear to be a substrate of CYP enzymes. The proposed metabolism of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is presented in Figure 24.
L2389: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L2390: Figure 24. In Vitro and In Vivo Metabolism of Ceftobiprole Medocaril Sodium
L2391: Chemical structures illustrating the metabolism of Ceftobiprole Medocaril Sodium (BAL5788).

BAL5788 (Ceftobiprole medocaril) undergoes metabolism:

- Decarboxylation yields \text{CO}_2 and Diacetyl.
- Diacetyl is metabolized to Acetoin, which is further metabolized to \text{CO}_2 and 2,3-Butanediol.
- Hydrolysis of the \beta-lactam ring yields BAL9141 (Ceftobiprole).
- BAL9141 undergoes ring opening to form BAL1029 (Open-ring metabolite of ceftobiprole).

L2393: ## 14.1.4. Potential for CYP Enzyme-Mediated Drug-Drug Interactions
L2394: No clinical drug-drug interaction studies of ceftobiprole have been performed.
L2395: In vitro CYP inhibition data (ceftobiprole concentration up to 200 \mu\text{M}; 107 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}) are summarized in Table 203. Only a slight (6% to 28%) inhibitory potential was apparent in the highest concentration range tested (50 to 200 \mu\text{M}; 26.7 to 107 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}; 1009572, FK6366, and FK6604). Ceftobiprole was not a time-dependent inhibitor of prototypical CYP substrates at the highest concentrations tested (200 \mu\text{M}; 107 \mu\text{g}/\text{mL}; studies FK6366 and FK6604). Due to solubility constraints, subsequent attempts to evaluate the direct and metabolism-dependent in vitro inhibition of human CYP enzymes at higher concentrations of ceftobiprole were unsuccessful (Study FK5807).

L2403: ## 14.1.5. Potential for Transporter-Mediated Drug-Drug Interactions
L2404: ## Ceftobiprole as a Substrate Of P-Glycoprotein and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein
L2405: In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of drug (efflux) transporters P-gp and breast cancer resistance protein in a bidirectional permeability assay across MDCKII cells (studies FK5942, XT138008, and XT228043). The bi-directional permeability of ceftobiprole (1, 10, and 100 µM; 0.535, 7.14, and 53.5 µg/mL) across MDCKII-MDR1, MDCKII-BCRP and control cells was low at all conditions (less than 3 x 10-6 cm/sec, similar to the control). The net efflux ratio of ceftobiprole was ≤2 at all concentrations and on all cell lines suggesting that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of either P-gp or BCRP.
L2406: ## Ceftobiprole as a Substrate of the Hepatic Transporters Organic Anion Transporter P1B1, Organic Anion Transporter P1B3, and Organic Cation Transporter 1
L2407: In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the hepatic uptake transporters OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and OCT1 (Studies XT138008 and XT228043).
L2408: In Study XT138008, ceftobiprole (1, 5, and 10 µM; 0.535, 2.68, and 7.14 µg/mL) was incubated with transporter (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1) expressing cells and control cells.
L2409: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L2410: Ceftobiprole did not accumulate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great extent and did not appear to be a substrate for OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1.
L2411: In Study XT228043, ceftobiprole (0.084, 0.24, 0.84, 2.4, 8.4, 28 and 84 \muM) was incubated with OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 transporter expressing cells and control cells. Ceftobiprole did not show accumulation of probe substrate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great extent with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) above 84 \muM. The uptake ratio of 84 \muM (44.5 \mug/mL) ceftobiprole was less than two in the absence of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 inhibitors. These results indicated that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 at 84 \muM but results at lower concentrations were inconclusive.
L2412: ## **Ceftobiprole as a Substrate Of The Renal Transporters Organic Cation Transporter 1, Organic Cation Transporter 3, and Organic Cation Transporter 2**
L2413: In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the renal transporters OAT1, OAT3, and OCT2 (Study XT138008). The highest concentration feasible to be tested in these assays was 10 \muM (7.14 \mug/mL). Ceftobiprole accumulated in OAT1 and OCT2 expressing cells at higher levels than control cells, suggesting it may be a possible substrate of those two transporters. However, the results should be interpreted with caution, as the amount of compound that accumulated in the cells was very low, which can have a large impact on the results.
L2414: ## **Ceftobiprole as a Substrate of the Transporters BSEP, and MRP2**
L2415: In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control vesicles in the presence and the absence of ATP were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the efflux transporters BSEP and MRP2. Ceftobiprole (1, 5, and 10 \muM; 0.535, 2.68, and 7.14 \mug/mL) did not accumulate in MRP2 or BSEP expressing vesicles in the presence of ATP at levels greater than in the absence of ATP suggesting it is not a substrate of either MRP2 or BSEP (Study XT138008).
L2416: ## **Ceftobiprole as an Inhibitor of Transporters**
L2417: In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of drug efflux transporters P-gp and BCRP in a bidirectional permeability assay across Caco-2 cells and/or MDCKII cells (Studies FK5942, XT138008, and XT228043). The potential for ceftobiprole to inhibit P-gp was evaluated in a MDR-MDCK cell assay using digoxin as the probe substrate. The permeability of digoxin in the presence and absence of ceftobiprole did not show any increase in the presence of 40 \muM (21.4 \mug/mL) ceftobiprole. The efflux ratios did not change significantly. As such, the results indicated that ceftobiprole is not a P-gp inhibitor. Similarly, ceftobiprole did not reduce the net efflux ratio of prazosin across MDCKII-BCRP and control cells, suggesting it is not an inhibitor of BCRP in vitro.
L2418: In vitro experiments (Studies XT138008, XT228043) were also conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of uptake transporters OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, OCT2, OAT1, and OAT3 and of efflux transporters MATE1 and MATE2-K by measuring the accumulation of a probe substrate in a transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells.
L2419: At the concentrations tested (0.3 to 200 \muM; 0.16 to 107 \mug/mL) (XT138008), ceftobiprole inhibited the accumulation of estradiol glucuronide in the OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 expressing
L2420: cells with IC50 values of 67.6 and 44.1 µM (36.14 µg/mL and 23.57 µg/mL), respectively. In a second study (study XT228043), ceftobiprole IC50 for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibition were determined to be above 84 µM (44.5 µg/mL, maximum achievable concentration). An investigational drug has the potential to inhibit OATP1B1/3 in vivo if the R value is &gt;1.1. The R values for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 were 1.50 and 1.76, respectively. Thus, ceftobiprole may increase concentrations of drugs eliminated by OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. Since the in vitro studies indicate that a drug is an OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 inhibitor, we recommend the Applicant conduct an in vivo drug interaction study evaluating ceftobiprole as an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATB1B3 transporters as a post-marketing requirement (see Section 8.2.1).
L2421: Ceftobiprole was not an inhibitor of MATE1, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, or OCT2 as it did not show accumulation of probe substrate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great extent with IC50 were above 84 µM (44.5 µg/mL) (Studies XT138008 and XT228043).
L2422: It was not possible to determine the inhibition potential of ceftobiprole on MATE2-K due to possible solvent-related issues with the in vitro assay (Study XT228043).
L2423: In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of efflux transporters BSEP and MRP2 by measuring the accumulation of a probe substrate (taurocholic acid or estradiol glucuronide) in vesicles in the presence of ceftobiprole (Study XT138008). The transport of taurocholic acid was reduced to less than 25% of the control in the presence of all concentrations of ceftobiprole (0.3 to 200 µM; 0.16 to 107 µg/mL) indicating that the IC50 could be lower than 0.3 µM. The Applicant attributes this inhibition to the acetic acid in the incubation that could have had an effect on the activity. Ceftobiprole did not inhibit the MRP2 mediated transport of estradiol 17-\beta-D-glucuronide.
L2424: ## 14.2. In Vivo Studies
L2425: ## 14.2.1. Single Ascending Dose
L2426: ## Study NP16104
L2427: NP16104 was a phase 1 single-center, single-dose, open-label, intra-subject, dose-escalation study in three healthy male volunteers aged 18 to 30 years. Each subject received single 30-min infusions of 250 mg, 500 mg, and 750 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium with a washout period of 72 hours between treatments.
L2428: Blood samples were collected prior to each drug administration and up to 24 hours after start of infusion. Urine was collected pre-dose and up to 24 hours post-dose. Ceftobiprole and ceftobiprole medocaril sodium were quantified using a validated high-performance liquid chromatography method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental and 2-compartmental methods. Plasma and urine PK parameters of ceftobiprole are summarized in Table 204 and Table 205, respectively.
L2429: Plasma concentrations of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium at the end of the infusion amounted to only 2% to 4% of those of the active principle, ceftobiprole. Thus, the PK of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium could not be determined.

L2443: ## **Study BAP00006**
L2444: BAP00006 was a phase 1, single-center, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled single, ascending dose study involving five sequential dose levels of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. In total, 40 healthy, male subjects between the ages of 20 and 40 years old were randomly assigned to one of the following five dose groups: 125, 250, 500, 750, or 1000 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. Each dose group included 8 subjects (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, n = 6; placebo, n = 2).
L2445: Blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and at up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Subjects were asked to void urine immediately before starting the first urine collection interval, 2 hours before dosing. Subsequently, urine was collected at -2 to 0 h (control) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated by use of a validated LC/LC-MS/MS method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental and two-compartmental methods. A one-way analysis of variance was used to assess dose-proportionality. The mean (standard deviation [SD]) %FT &gt;

L2465: ## **Study BAP00036**
L2466: BAP00036 was a single dose, single center, open-label, comparative study with 24 healthy subjects, 12 females and 12 males. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium at a dose of 750 mg (ceftobiprole equivalents) was administered as a single 30-minute intravenous infusion on Study Day 1. Blood samples were collected 15 to 30 minutes before infusion start and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Urine was collected at -2 to 0 hour (control and last portion of the 24-hour urine collection on Study Day -1) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated by a validated LC-MS/MS method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental methods.
L2467: Pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary recovery for ceftobiprole following single intravenous administration of 750 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium in healthy male and female subjects are summarized in Table 208. L2468: Because ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was not measurable in most plasma samples obtained after infusion, no PK evaluation was possible. Assessment of lactam ring open metabolite BAL2070 was not performed.

L2475: ## **Study BAP00210**
L2476: BAP00210 was a single-center, open-label, randomized, parallel group, single-dose phase 1 study. A total of 36 subjects (18 male, 18 female) were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to one of two dosing regimens: ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (as ceftobiprole equivalents) 750 mg infused over 30 minutes or 500 mg infused over 60 minutes. Each dosing regimen included 18 (9 male, 9 female) subjects. Blood samples were collected on Study Day 1 immediately before start of infusion and up to 24 hours after start of infusion. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated using a validated LC/LC-MS/MS method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental methods. Time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (T &gt; MIC) was determined using 4 µg/mL as an MIC value and 12 hours as the dosing interval.
L2477: Pharmacokinetic parameters for ceftobiprole following single intravenous administration of 500 mg and 750 mg infusions of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium in healthy subjects are summarized Table 209.

L2491: ## **Study CSI-1004**
L2492: CSU-1004 was a single center, open-label study in a total of 28 healthy men and nonpregnant women between the ages of 18 and 55 years, inclusive. Subjects received a total of 8 intravenous doses (1 single dose and 7 multiple doses) at approximately the same time(s) each day during the study. Each dose of 500 mg ceftobiprole was infused over a 2-hour period. On Day 1, a single dose was administered; 3 doses were each administered on Days 3 and Day 4, and 1 dose was infused on Day 5.
L2493: Blood for PK analysis was collected for 24 hours following the infusions on Days 1 and 5, before each infusion on Days 3 and 4, and at the end of each infusion on Day 4. Urine was collected for 48 hours after dosing on Day 1 and up to 24 hours after dosing on Day 5.
L2494: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole plasma and urine concentrations were assayed using validated LC-MS/MS method. Pharmacokinetic parameters of ceftobiprole and/or the open-ring metabolite were estimated on Days 1 and 5. Accumulation ratio was calculated by AUC_t on Day 5/AUC_t on Day 1. In addition, the percentage of time at which ceftobiprole was above the MIC for the duration of the dosing interval (%T&gt;MIC) was calculated for each individual and summarized descriptively.

L2545: ## 14.2.2. Multiple Ascending Dose
L2546: ## Study BAP00010
L2547: BAP00006 was a phase 1, single-center, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled multiple ascending dose study involving two dose levels of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (500 mg and 750 mg of ceftobiprole equivalents).
L2548: Sixteen subjects were randomly assigned to one of the two dose groups. Each dose group included 8 subjects (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, n = 6; placebo, n = 2). A third dose group (1000 mg) was planned but no subjects received this dose, due to the occurrence of elevated liver transaminase levels in approximately 50% of subjects dosed with placebo or ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. Adverse changes were noted in 2 of 4 subjects receiving placebo and in 7 of 12 subjects receiving BAL5788 at 500 mg (3 of 6 subjects) or 750 mg (4 of 6 subjects).
L2549: On Study Days 1 and 8, blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. To determine the trough levels of ceftobiprole, blood samples were collected before the morning infusion on Study Days 3, 5, and 7. Urine was collected at -2 to 0 hours (control) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion on Study Days 1 and 8.
L2550: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated by a validated LC/LC-MS/MS method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental and two-compartmental methods. Drug accumulation, R_{ACC}, was estimated by AUC_{0-12h} on Day 8 divided by AUC_{0-12h} on Day 1. Time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (T &gt; MIC) was determined (MIC_{90} for MRSA = 2 \mug/mL). A one-way analysis of variance was used to assess dose-proportionality.
L2551: Pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary recovery for ceftobiprole following multiple intravenous administration of 500 and 750 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium in healthy, male subjects are summarized in
L2552: **Table 215.** The mean (SD) %T&gt;MIC for subjects receiving 500 mg was 47.9 (4.2) on Day 1 and 49.9 (5.3) on Day 8. The mean (SD) %T&gt;MIC for subjects receiving 750 mg was 61.2 (5.4) on Day 1 and 62.5 (4.4) on Day 8.

L2563: ## Study BAP00058
L2564: BAP00058 was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, multiple dose study, conducted at a single center. Twelve male subjects were randomly assigned to receive ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (750 mg of ceftobiprole equivalents; 6 subjects) or placebo (6 subjects) as intravenous (i.v.) infusions for 12 days. Administration was once daily on Days 1 and 12 in order to allow 24-hour sampling for PK, and was twice daily, every 12 hours, on Days 2 to 11.
L2565: On Days 1 and 12, blood samples were collected immediately before start of infusion and up to 24 hours after infusion start. Subjects were encouraged to void urine at the end of each collection interval, i.e., at 0, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours.
