L2578: ## 14.2.3. Renal Impairment
L2579: BAP00018 was a phase 1, single-center, open-label, non-randomized parallel group study. Twenty male subjects (5 per group) were enrolled into the following groups according to their creatinine clearance (CL_{CR}) determined at screening:
L2580: - Group A (normal renal function: CL_{CR} &gt;80 mL/min),
- Group B (mild renal impairment: CL_{CR} = 51-80 mL/min),
- Group C (moderate renal impairment: CL_{CR} = 30-50 mL/min), and
- Group D (severe renal impairment: CL_{CR} &lt;30 mL/min)
L2581: On study Day 1, each subject received a single dose ceftobiprole medocaril sodium 30 minutes. Blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Urine was collected at -2 to 0 hours (control and last portion of the 24-hour urine collection on Study Day -1) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion.
L2582: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated by a validated LC/LC-MS/MS method. Pharmacokinetic parameters were derived by non-compartmental and two-compartmental methods. Time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (T &gt; MIC) was determined; in these calculations, the dosing interval was defined as 12 hours (corresponding to twice daily administration), and the MIC value defined as 4 µg/mL, since this is the highest MIC for ceftobiprole in the case of MRSA.

L2593: *Of note, mean age differed between the groups (specifically, the renally impaired groups versus normal subjects), as follows: normal subjects, 23.8 \pm 3.9 years; subjects with mild impairment, 44.6 \pm 9.2 years; subjects with moderate impairment, 47.2 \pm 15.3 years; and subjects with severe impairment, 55.8 \pm 5.36 years. The Applicant did not study the effect of age in a Phase 1 healthy volunteer study. Age was not identified as a significant covariate affecting ceftobiprole PK in adults (see Section 14.5).*
L2594: Study CSI-1007 was a single-dose PK study in subjects with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Twelve subjects were enrolled in this study: six healthy male subjects with normal renal function and six male subjects with ESRD (CL_{CR} of 0 to 15 mL/min) on hemodialysis. Healthy subjects were enrolled after all ESRD subjects had completed the study and were matched on a 1:1 basis by age and weight.
L2595: Healthy subjects were given a single 2-hour infusion of 250 mg ceftobiprole; subjects with ESRD on hemodialysis were given a 2-hour infusion of 250 mg ceftobiprole 3 hours before dialysis in Period 1 and immediately after dialysis in Period 2, with a washout period of at least 14 days between periods.
L2596: Blood and urine samples were collected for up to 48 hours post-dose administration. Venous blood samples were collected immediately before the infusion, during the infusion, and up to 48 hours after the start of infusion in all subjects and all periods. Venous blood samples were also collected before and at the end (4 hours) of the hemodialysis on Day 3 and Day 5 in ESRD subjects in Period 1 and Period 2. Arterial blood samples were taken at 4, 5, 6, and 7 hours during the 4-hour hemodialysis in ESRD subjects in Period 1. During this time frame, dialysate samples were also collected every 30 minutes. Additional pre-dose, 2-hour blood, and 24 hours post-start of the infusion blood samples were taken on Day 1 for the determination of plasma protein binding by ultra-filtration.
L2597: Urine was collected before the infusion and over the intervals of 0 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 24, and 24 to 48 hours after the infusion in healthy subjects only.

L2608: The reviewer identified that the plasma concentration data for ceftobiprole dosed after hemodialysis was switched between 30 min and 90 min in the Applicant's report. L2611: ## 14.2.4. Obesity
L2612: CSI-1008 was an open-label, single-dose, parallel-group PK study of ceftobiprole in morbidly obese and non-obese subjects. Twenty-five (12 morbidly obese, defined as a BMI of \ge 40 kg/m^2, and 13 demographically-matched non-obese, defined as a BMI between 18 and 30 kg/m^2) subjects were enrolled in the study and received a single 2-hour infusion of 500 mg ceftobiprole. The mean weight and BMI were 130.9 kg and 45.5 kg/m^2 for morbidly obese subjects and 73.5 kg and 24 kg/m^2 for non-obese subjects, respectively.
L2613: Blood and urine were collected pre-dose and up to 24 hours following the end of infusion. Plasma, ultra-filtrate, and urine samples were analyzed for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, ceftobiprole and the open-ring metabolite using a validated LC-MS/MS method.
L2614: Ceftobiprole AUC was approximately 17% lower among morbidly obese compared to non-obese subjects (Table 219).

L2633: ## 14.2.5. Drug Penetration
L2634: ## Soft Tissue Penetration
L2635: CSI-1002 was an exploratory study to evaluate the penetration of ceftobiprole into soft tissue determined by in vivo microdialysis in healthy subjects.
L2636: This Study was conducted in two sequential parts: a pilot study and a main study. The pilot study was conducted in 3 control subjects. Ceftobiprole was locally administered via microdialysis followed by a washout period of 3 hours during which dialysate samples were taken every 30 minutes for 4 hours.
L2637: The main study was conducted in 12 healthy subjects. Ceftobiprole was administered locally via microdialysis followed by a washout period of 3 hours. After the washout period, each subject received a single 2-hour IV infusion of 500 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. Dialysate samples were collected pre-dose and every 20 min from start of infusion through 12 hours post-start of dosing. Blood samples were collected at time 0 (pre-dose) up to 24 hours after the start of the infusion.
L2638: Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium concentrations were only assessed in plasma. Protein binding in plasma was determined by ultra-filtration at pre-dose, 2, and 12 hours after the start of the infusion. Concentrations of ceftobiprole in dialysate were quantified using a validated high-performance liquid chromatography/ultraviolet method.
L2639: Individual PK parameters for ceftobiprole in plasma, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue are summarized in Table 221. Penetration of ceftobiprole into soft tissues was demonstrated and was 69% of the unbound plasma exposure for skeletal muscle and 49% of the unbound plasma exposure for adipose tissue.

L2648: ## Lung Penetration
L2649: CSI-1005 was an exploratory, open-label study to assess the bronchoalveolar distribution and PK of ceftobiprole administered as 500 mg every 8 hours to healthy adult subjects.
L2650: Twenty-eight healthy subjects were enrolled to receive ceftobiprole and undergo bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sampling. Of these, 25 were evaluable for PK and 24 subjects underwent the BAL procedure. Two control subjects were enrolled to undergo the BAL procedure only to validate the bioanalytical assay and did not receive ceftobiprole. All subjects, except for the control subjects, received four 2-hour infusions of ceftobiprole (500 mg) 8 hours apart. Following the fourth infusion, a single BAL sample was collected in each subject at either 2.5, 4, 6, or 8 hours after the start of the infusion.
L2651: Blood samples were also collected in all pre-dose and up to 8 hours after the start of the infusion. Ceftobiprole concentrations in plasma and BAL fluid was quantified using a validated LC-MS/MS method.
L2652: Overall penetration in ELF and alveolar macrophages (as measured by the AUC ratio of the tissue concentration to the unbound plasma concentration) was 16% and 2%, respectively. Plasma and BAL ceftobiprole concentrations are outlined in Table 222 and Table 223, respectively.

L2682: ## 14.5. Pharmacometrics Assessment
L2683: ## 14.5.1. Population PK Analysis
L2684: ## 14.5.1.1. Review Summary
L2685: In this submission, the Applicant performed population PK (PopPK analyses including phase 3 studies in adult subjects with SAB, ABSSSIs, and CABP). PopPK analyses were also performed for pediatric subjects.
L2686: In general, the Applicant's PopPK analyses (for SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP in adult subjects and for CABP in pediatric subjects) are considered acceptable for the characterization of ceftobiprole disposition and evaluation of covariate impacts. The PopPK models were also acceptable for the generation of exposure metrics for exposure-efficacy analyses, clinical scenario simulations, and PTA analyses. Overall, the PopPK, PK/PD, and PTA analysis results support dosage selections for the indicated general and special populations requiring dosage adjustments. The Applicant's analyses were verified by the reviewer, with no significant discordance identified. Specifically, the developed models corresponding to the indications were used to support the current submission as outlined in Table 225. Of note, the labeling language reflects review team conclusions at the time of writing this review but may not reflect the finalized labeling language.
L2687: Table 225. Specific Comments on Applicant's Final Population PK model
L2688: Utility of the Final Model	Reviewer's Comments
Support Applicant's proposed labeling statements about intrinsic and extrinsic factors	Intrinsic factor	
Section 8.5 Geriatric Use
No dosage adjustment is required for elderly patients. Dosage adjustment for elderly patients should be based on renal function.
Section 8.6 Renal Impairment
Adult Patients
The ZEVTERA dosage is reduced in adult patients with CL_{CR} < 50 mL/min, including patients with a CL_{CR} < 15 mL/min either receiving or not receiving hemodialysis.
Renal impairment (CL_{CR} < 50 mL/min) increases ceftobiprole AUC in adult patients, which may increase the risk of ZEVTERA adverse reactions.
Pediatric Patients
The ZEVTERA dosage is reduced in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with renal impairment (eGFR 15 to < 50 mL/min/1.73 m^2).
Use in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with renal impairment (eGFR 15 to < 50 mL/min/1.73 m^2) is predicted to increase ceftobiprole AUC, which may increase the risk of ZEVTERA adverse reactions. The effect of any degree of renal impairment in pediatric patients younger than 2 years of age or in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with an eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m^2 either receiving or not receiving hemodialysis on ceftobiprole PK is unknown.
8.7 Augmented Renal Clearance
Increase the ZEVTERA dosing frequency in adult patients with augmented renal clearance (CL_{CR} > 150 mL/min).
Use in adult patients with augmented renal clearance (CL_{CR} > 150 mL/min) is predicted to decrease ceftobiprole exposure, which may reduce ZEVTERA efficacy. The effect of augmented renal clearance function (CL_{CR} > 150 mL/min) on ceftobiprole PK in pediatric patients is unknown.
Section 12.3 Pharmacokinetics
Specific Populations
No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adults based on age (18 to 91 years), gender (36% female), or race/ethnicity (88% White, 3% Black, 5% Asian). The effect of hepatic impairment on ceftobiprole PK is unknown.
Based on population PK modeling, exposure-efficacy analyses, Monte Carlo simulations, and probability of target attainment analyses, these statements are acceptable to support dosing recommendations.
The population PK models demonstrate that no clinically significant impacts are observed on the PK of ceftobiprole based on age, gender, or race/ethnicity. No patients with hepatic impairment were evaluated in the population PK modeling.
L2689: Patients with Renal Impairment
No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adult subjects and subjects with mild renal impairment (CL_{CR} 50 to 80 mL/min). Ceftobiprole AUC increased 2.5-fold in adult subjects with moderate renal impairment (CL_{CR} 30 to < 50 mL/min) and 3.3-fold in severe renal impairment (CL_{CR} < 30 mL/min).
End-stage Renal Disease Requiring Dialysis
No clinically significant difference in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in adult patients with ESRD (CL_{CR} < 15 mL/min) compared to healthy adult subjects based on limited PK data and PK modeling and simulation.
Patients with Augmented Renal Clearance
A clinically significant reduction in ceftobiprole exposure is predicted in adult patients with augmented renal clearance (CL_{CR} > 150 mL/min) based upon a mechanistic understanding of this drug. The effect of augmented renal clearance (CL_{CR} > 150 mL/min) on ceftobiprole PK in pediatric patients is unknown.
Pediatric Use
No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed between pediatric patients from (b) (4) to < 18 years with normal renal function following administration of an intravenous dose of ZEVTERA.

L2722: ## **Base Model**
L2723: The final base model was a 3-compartment PK model with linear elimination from the central compartment, and baseline creatinine clearance (CLcr) was included on CL *a priori*. Additive error models (in the log domain) were separate for phase 1 and phase 3 studies. The model structure is shown in Figure 26.
L2724: Interindividual variability (IIV) was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient level random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined. Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of goodness-of-fit (GoF) such as a decrease in the minimum objective function value (OFV), accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model convergence, and diagnostic plots.

L2733: Forward selection and backwards elimination steps were undertaken during Applicant's model development. Clinical judgment, physiologic relevance, and mechanistic plausibility were applied. Continuous covariates were evaluated using a power function and categorical covariates were parameterized as a fractional change.

L2755: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L2756: *The reviewer was able to reproduce the Applicant's final PopPK model for ABSSSI and CABP subjects. The Applicant's final model is acceptable in describing the ceftobiprole PK characteristics pooling phase 1 and phase 3 subjects. The model qualification is demonstrated*
L2757: *through precision of parameter estimates (all %SEM under 12.1% except one parameter at 21.9%) and alignment of resampled parameter estimates (90% CI contains model parameter estimates). Additionally, there is no obvious bias or misspecification in the GoF plots for the final model (observed vs. predicted concentrations show good agreements and mostly align with the line of unity; the CWRES scatter around y = 0 without obvious trends). The NPDE and prediction-corrected VPC plots show that the final model is able to capture the observed data; however, when the prediction-corrected VPC plot is further stratified by phase 1 vs. phase 3 subjects, the phase 3 prediction-corrected VPC plot demonstrates bias beyond 8 hours (Figure 30), and this is likely due to the relatively sparse PK available in that time frame in phase 3 studies.*
L2758: *Of note, the Applicant fixed the nosocomial pneumonia effect (NP) on CL to zero in the final model. As such, the reviewer performed a sensitivity analysis by re-estimating this parameter to assess the impact of NP on CL. The resulting model did not provide statistically meaningful improvement over the Applicant's final model (minimal change in OFV). This is likely due to the relatively low percent of NP subjects (5.69%) in the pooled dataset. Overall, the Applicant's final covariate model is acceptable in describing ceftobiprole disposition, in deriving exposure metrics for exposure-response analysis, and in simulating for target attainment analysis in adult subjects with ABSSSI or CABP.*

L2826: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L2827: The reviewer was able to reproduce the Applicant's refined PopPK model for SAB (i.e., final model). The final parameter estimates were precise (all %SEM under 13.3% except CL shift for SAB was moderate at 36.7%) and aligned with the resampled parameter estimates (90% confidence interval [CI] contains model parameter estimates). Similar to the final PopPK model for ABSSSI and CABP, there is no obvious bias or misspecification observed in the GoF plots (observed vs. predicted concentrations show good agreements and mostly align with the line of unity; the CWRES scatter around y = 0 without obvious trends). The NPDE and prediction-corrected VPC plots show that the refined SAB PopPK model can capture the observed data; however, when the prediction-corrected VPC plot is limited to SAB subjects, some under-predictions are shown and are more prominent beyond 8 hours. This is likely due to the relatively sparse PK available in the 8-to-24-hour timeframe (based on time from last dose). Overall, the model reasonably captures central tendency of the SAB PK data. The Applicant's final SAB model is acceptable in describing ceftobiprole disposition, in deriving exposure metrics for exposure-response analysis for the SAB population, and in simulating for target attainment analysis (i.e., PTA) in adult subjects with SAB.
L2828: In the phase 3 trial in SAB subjects, a total of 21 subjects with ESRD were randomized to continue iHD renal replacement modality while receiving ceftobiprole (n=20 in the final NONMEM dataset); however, the reviewer noted in the Applicant's report that, "the exact times at which hemodialysis was started and stopped was not recorded, the trial protocol stipulated that drug dosing and PK sampling on the hemodialysis day was to occur after the completion of the hemodialysis session." The uncertainty regarding iHD effect in ESRD subjects is further complicated by the unreliable results of the dedicated phase 1 study in ESRD subjects (see discussion in Section 8. The Applicant suggested that the study protocol was likely followed
L2829: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L2830: based on: 1) PopPK model performance in this subgroup, 2) no obvious bias observed based on diagnostic plots of the PopPK model by ESRD status (Figure 38 and Figure 39); refer to Applicant's PopPK report and Information Request responses for additional plots), and 3) visual comparisons of concentration-time profiles of non-ESRD subjects vs. ESRD subjects not on iHD vs. ESRD subjects on iHD. Additionally, the Applicant's response to a follow-up Information Request indicated that 8 of the 20 subjects had confirmed administration and PK sampling times post iHD sessions. The reviewer agrees that these aspects overall may increase the confidence of the data to be used for comparison, model-based simulation, and dose selection in the setting of ESRD regardless of iHD because the doses are administered post dialysis sessions. One limitation to acknowledge is that model-based simulations cannot be conducted in the setting of iHD due to a lack of information for extraction ratio (i.e., unreliable phase 1 data). Despite this limitation, the SAB PTA results provide further support of the dosing selection in the ESRD population regardless of extraction ratio. Refer to Section 14.5.2.3 for further discussion of dosing recommendation. The Information Requests and responses related to ESRD can be found at these EDR links: IR_SEQ026, IR_SEQ036, and IR_SEQ041.
L2831: ## 14.5.1.5. Pediatrics CABP
L2832: ## 14.5.1.5.1. Model Development
L2833: The Applicant submitted 2 technical reports for the indicated pediatric age group for CABP (Report 00616-3 and Report 00616-3A). The first report utilized pediatric data only for PopPK model development (referred to as the original pediatric only PopPK model), and the latter report is an addendum to Report 00616-3 with pooled pediatric and adult data, including adult subjects with renal impairment. Per Applicant, this addendum was requested by the Swedish Medical Products Agency. While both reports were submitted under this NDA, emphasis is placed on the addendum report (i.e., 00616-3A) as the final model is used for exposure derivation, simulations, and PTA analysis to support dosing recommendation in pediatric subjects down to 3 months of age for CABP. The overall objectives of the analyses in pediatric subjects were to:
L2834: - Identity the renal function estimate equation that provides the best model fit to the observed PK data
- Develop a pediatric PopPK model using a pooled dataset of pediatric and adult subjects (including adults with renal impairment [RI])
- Provide dosing recommendations in pediatric subjects with renal impairment
L2835: ## Data
L2836: A total of 3 pediatric studies were included for pediatric PopPK model development. Study design and dosages are summarized in Table 236. For pediatric subjects, the final NONMEM dataset included 112 subjects who contributed 606 evaluable plasma concentrations. The pooled phase 1 adult PK data included an additional 187 subjects with 2,761 evaluable plasma concentrations in addition to the pediatric PK data. A summary of baseline characteristics for pediatric subjects included in the model development are provided in Table 237. Of note, the proposed indication in this NDA is down to 3 months of age.
L2837: In regard to estimation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in pediatric subjects, including those undergoing renal function maturation, the Applicant utilized 4 approaches for model fitting: 1) bedside Schwartz (mL/min/1.73 m2) (Schwartz et al. 2009), 2) Rhodin formula using normalized
L2838: NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L2839: fat mass (mL/min), 3) Rhodin formula using fat-free mass (mL/min) (Rhodin et al. 2009) and 4) renal maturation function using DeCock et al (De Cock et al. 2014).

L2852: ## Base Model
L2853: The original PopPK model structure was fitted to the pooled pediatric and adult dataset. The final base model (from pediatric data alone) was a linear 3-compartment with a direct relationship between renal clearance (CL) and GFR based on Rhodin and fat-free mass (GFRRhodin, FFM). Body weight was included on volume (estimated exponent) and clearance related terms (fixed exponent of 0.75). IIV was included on central volume of distribution (Vc) only.
L2854: For the final base model, IIV was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for subject level random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined. Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of GoF such as a decrease in the OFV, accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model convergence, and diagnostic plots.
L2855: ## Covariate Model
L2856: Covariate screening was undertaken via plots in the original pediatric only PopPK model, but no obvious relationships were observed. As such, no formal stepwise covariate modeling was
L2857: conducted (i.e., forward selection and backwards elimination) when the model was fitted to the pooled dataset.
L2858: ## 14.5.1.5.2. Final Model
L2859: The final PopPK model (revised with pooled data) has the same model structure as the final base model. The parameter estimates of the original and revised pediatric PopPK model are summarized in Table 238. The relationship between CL and GFR was estimated to be quite similar when fit to the pooled dataset (slope of 0.0555 vs. slope of 0.0548 from the pediatric model), and the population mean estimates for Q1 (intercompartmental flow from Vc to Vp1, volume of distribution for peripheral compartment 1) and Q2 (intercompartmental flow from Vc to Vp2, volume of distribution for peripheral compartment 2) were similar as well. The Applicant acknowledged that the addition of adult phase 1 data resulted in marked decreases in the population mean Vc and V1 estimates such that the population mean volume of distribution at steady-state (Vss) (i.e., sum of all volume of distribution terms) is calculated to be 17.3 L versus 71.7 L when the model was fit to the pediatric data alone. Prediction-correct VPC plots are shown in Figure 40, Figure 41, and Figure 42. A comparison of the two models is illustrated in Figure 43.

L2879: ## Reviewer Comments
L2880: *The original pediatric only PopPK model had reasonable model estimates (parameter precision of low to high standard error of the mean (%SEM) and low to moderate shrinkage for relevant parameters). When fitted to the pooled dataset of pediatric and phase 1 adult PK data, the renal elimination parameter was numerically similar and the ETA shrinkages were reduced; however, the volume of distribution terms had large numeric changes and large increase in %SEM. Overall, the prediction-corrected VPC plots demonstrate that the revised PopPK model is able to capture the central tendency of ceftobiprole PK in the target pediatric subject population of 3 month to &lt;18 years).*
L2881: *The reviewer performed a sensitivity analysis (not shown) with additional parameters to model the proportional shifts (from typical values) of clearance and volume of distribution related terms for pediatric vs. adult subjects. The final model parameter estimates are similar to those reported by the Applicant for the revised PopPK model with reduced %SEM values. Notably, the OFV values remain unchanged. In general, the Applicant's final PopPK model is acceptable for derivation of individual exposure metrics and used for Monte Carlo simulation to support dosing recommendation in subjects with normal renal function and those with renal impairment (for pediatric subjects aged 2 years and older).*

L2898: Of note, the CABP mITT analysis population included 2 subjects with *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* at baseline and with respective MIC values of &gt;16 and 4 \mug/mL (free-drug %T&gt;MIC of 0% and 80.5%) and 1 subject with *Acinetobacter baumannii* at baseline and an MIC value of 8 \mug/mL (free-drug %T&gt;MIC of 69.5%). The subject with *Acinetobacter baumannii* was the only subject with all-cause mortality within 30 days. For the ME Analysis Population, the subject with *P. aeruginosa* at baseline and an MIC value of 4 \mug/mL was the only one with free-drug plasma %T&gt;MIC &lt;99.2%. Given that the majority of subjects had %T&gt;MIC at the high end of the range, the exposure-efficacy analyses (univariable or multivariable) were not performed by the Applicant.

L2914: ## Reviewer Comments
L2915: *The distributions of free-drug %T&gt;MIC in the two analysis populations for ABSSSI and CABP being at or close to high end of the range likely indicate that the subjects were at the plateau of the exposure-efficacy relationships for ABSSSI and CABP infection types. When evaluated against nonclinical targets of %T&gt;MIC (Table 243), fewer subjects with gram-negative pathogens achieved the stasis, 1-log kill, and 2-log kill targets (range, 77.8% to 100%) when compared to those with gram-positive pathogens (range, 100%-100%). This is further evaluated in PTA analysis section to support dosing selection.*
L2916: ## **14.5.2.1.3. PTA**
L2917: Because the renal route is a major elimination pathway for ceftobiprole (and as described in the PopPK modeling section), the target attainment analysis utilized renal-based dosing groups to simulate ceftobiprole exposures to support dosing selection for ABSSSI and CABP. To simulate in a clinical scenario, virtual subjects resembling the respective subject populations (i.e., ABSSSI and CABP) were generated, and exposure metrics were derived from the virtual subjects. Note that given the lack of information on renal replacement modality impact on ceftobiprole PK (i.e., percent of drug being removed from iHD in the ceftobiprole development program), the Applicant's simulations were conducted without incorporating the extraction ratio (see Section 8 and Pharmacometric Assessment Appendix Section 14.5.1.4.2). Ceftobiprole dosing regimens for exposure derivation (via simulations) and PTA analyses are summarized in Table 244. For the PTA analysis, the nonclinical PK/PD targets are summarized in Section 5. The randomly assigned targets were derived based on an estimated log normal distribution of %T&gt;MIC targets associated with a given endpoint (truncated within 2 standard deviations of the mean value).
L2918: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L2919: *For pathogens causing ABSSSI or CABP, the PTA analyses (based on median and random targets) demonstrate that the proposed dosing regimen (across renal function groups) provides sufficient coverage up to an MIC of 4 µg/mL for 1-log kill across MIC distributions for respective gram-positive pathogens; for gram-negative pathogens, the exposures cover up to an MIC of 2 µg/mL for 1-log kill.*

L3032: ## 14.5.2.2. *Staphylococcus aureus* Bacteremia PK/PD Analysis
L3033: ## 14.5.2.2.1. Introduction
L3034: The Applicant performed PK/PD analyses for the SAB populations with the following objects:
L3035: - To evaluate exposure-efficacy relationships using the refined PopPK model for SAB
- To conduct PTA to support ceftobiprole dosing regimens and susceptibility testing interpretive criteria against *S. aureus*
L3036: ## 14.5.2.2.2. Exposure-Efficacy Analysis
L3037: Exposure-efficacy relationship was evaluated for SAB using PK and clinical data from Trial BPR-CS-008. Dosing regimens administered in SAB subjects are summarized in Table 262. The primary endpoint was overall success in the treatment of SAB, including infective endocarditis, at the post-treatment evaluation (PTE) visit (Day 70 +/- 5 post-randomization) in the mITT population (defined as *the subset of subjects in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population who received any amount of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive for S. aureus at baseline based on a central microbiology laboratory assessment*). Overall success is defined if the following criteria were met:
L3038: - Subject was alive at PTE visit;
- No new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection;
- Resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms; and
- Two negative blood cultures for *S. aureus*
- At least one while subject was on active study treatment, and
- confirmed by at least one subsequent negative blood culture for *S. aureus* (either in the period between 7 days after the end-of-treatment (EOT) visit and PTE visit or at the PTE visit)
L3039: The Applicant employed two analysis populations for the exposure-efficacy analysis: 1) mITT population with baseline pathogen, microbiological data, and sufficient PK data and 2) a subpopulation of the first analysis population with *S. aureus* isolated at baseline. A total of 174 and 172 subjects were included in the mITT and mITT *S. aureus* analysis populations, respectively. Refer to the Applicant's PK/PD report (Tables 10 and 11 in the submitted report) for a summary of baseline characteristics of the analysis populations. The response for efficacy endpoints by visits in two analysis populations are summarized in Table 263. Ceftobiprole MIC, free-drug AUC, and Day 1 free-drug plasma %T&gt;MIC for both analysis populations are summarized in Table 264. Percent of subjects in each analysis population achieving nonclinical targets is summarized in Table 265. Given that individual %T&gt;MIC aggregate at the high end of respective ranges, the exposure-efficacy analyses (univariable or multivariable) were not performed by the Applicant.
L3040: Of note, two subjects had *A. baumannii* and *C. striatum* selected as baseline pathogens with MICs of &gt;64 and &gt;16 µg/mL, respectively. For these two subjects, the free-drug %T&gt;MIC were of 0% on Days 1 and 10 and were categorized as failures regarding overall success endpoints at EOT and PTE. While the free-drug plasma %T&gt;MIC with respect to the baseline *S. aureus*
L3041: ## NDA 218275
## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L3042: pathogens for these two subjects was 98.8%, the Applicant postulated that the clinical failure was potentially due to the other pathogens or other subject variables.

L3060: The reviewer also examined the exposures (i.e., free-drug AUC) and free-drug %T&gt;MIC on Days 1 and 10 for subjects with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE) as assessed by investigators in the mITT population. L3118: ## 14.5.2.3. Assessment of End-Stage Renal Disease Dosing Regimen for Adults
L3119: For adult subjects with ESRD (on or not on iHD), 250 mg IV q24h is the recommended dosing regimen (for all indications); however, model-based simulations show that the exposure (i.e., Day 1 AUC) may be suboptimal in ESRD subjects (not on iHD) with renal function of 0-15 mL/min when compared to those with normal renal function (defined as 90-150 mL/min) in ABSSSI (Figure 45). Numerically lower model-predicted exposures on Day 1 are also seen with CABP and SAB infection types. As such, an Information Request was communicated to the Applicant to compare ESRD dosing (not on iHD) at q12h vs. q24h dosing frequencies and provide safety assessment for the q12h dosing regimen.
L3120: While the q12h dosing may seem reasonable based on Day 1 exposure metrics, the exposures (after multiple-day administrations) on Day 5 for SAB and Day 7 for ABSSSI and CABP are higher than those observed to date in clinical and nonclinical studies (Table 275). Additionally, the Applicant stated that there has been no clinical safety experience at the predicted exposures that would be reached based on the q12h dosing regimen in ESRD subjects.
L3121: Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L3122: Despite lower exposures at the proposed dosing regimen at q24h on Day 1, the accumulation  observed in simulated ESRD subjects after 5 days of ceftobiprole administrations for the  proposed dosing regimen led to exposures in a similar range to that observed in simulated  subjects with normal renal function. Furthermore, the PTA results (representative PTA results for  SAB based on the median target for 1-log kill is provided in Table 276) demonstrate that the  q24h still provide sufficient exposure (&gt;90% probability of target attainment) across SAB,  ABSSSI, and CABP infection types (refer to the Applicant's response to Information Request for  additional PTA results).

L3128: ## **Reviewer Comments**
L3129: *In the setting of iHD, the exact exposures are difficult to predict due to a lack of dedicated phase 1 study data to confirm the extraction ratio. As such, no modeling and simulations can be conducted with the extraction ratio from iHD to predict the concentrations over time. If a conservative measure of assuming 100% of ceftobiprole is removed during iHD sessions, the ceftobiprole administered post-dialysis would have been similar to the exposures derived on Day 1 as shown in Table 275. Moreover, these model-predicted exposures achieved similar probability target attainments values of &gt;90%. In general, the ESRD dosing of 250 mg IV q24h in the setting of iHD (administered post-dialysis) is acceptable. Refer to Section II.8.1.2 for discussions.*

L3186: ## 14.5.2.5. Assessment of Severe Renal Impairment Dosing Regimen for Adolescents
L3187: Based on the submitted PK/PD report for pediatric subjects for the CABP indication (Report 00616-3), a dose of 7.5 mg/kg q24h (up to 500 mg) was recommended for adolescents 12 to &lt;18 years of age; however, the Applicant proposes the same weight-based dosing at q12h dosing frequency (i.e., 7.5 mg/kg q12h, up to 250 mg) in the severe RI category. As such, an Information Request (dated 5 FEBRUARY 2024; link) was communicated to the Applicant. Briefly, the Applicant stated that the decision to modify from q24h to q12h was to align with adult dosing regimen for severe RI through interactions with the European Health Authorities. Additionally, the Applicant provided further simulations to support the q12h dosing regimen in this population as summarized in Table 282. At a dosing frequency of q12h (capped at 250 mg per dose), the exposures based on AUC would be slightly higher and the C_{max} slightly lower in adolescent subjects with severe RI (AUC = 259 \mu g \cdot h/mL; C_{max} = 20.7 \mu g/mL) than the exposures predicted in subjects with q24h dosing frequency (AUC = 240 \mu g \cdot h/mL; C_{max} = 24.6 \mu g/mL). Overall, the change in dosing frequency results in an improvement in PTA results.

Overall, the proposed 7.5 mg/kg q12h dosing for adolescents with severe RI is acceptable.

L3201: ## 17. Clinical Safety
L3202: ## 17.1. Phase 1 Studies
L3203: The Applicant submitted eighteen adult phase 1 and two pediatric phase 1 studies for ceftobiprole. The population of these studies include healthy subjects, subjects on hemodialysis, subjects with impaired renal function and end-stage renal disease, morbidly obese subjects, subjects who underwent elective hip replacement surgery, and subjects who were hospitalized in intensive or intermediate care units. These studies covered a dose range of 125 mg to 1000 mg.
L3204: There were no deaths in the phase 1 healthy adult studies. However, there were two adult subjects in the intensive care unit phase 1 studies who died due to the unrelated adverse events (AEs) of septic shock and intracranial hemorrhage. SAEs were reported for eight subjects (none in healthy adults). The only SAE which was considered related to the study drug was acute kidney injury. The most common AEs experienced in this population were nausea (29.6%), taste disorder (21%), headache (16.6%), and vomiting (11.2%). Additional AEs that occurred in &gt;2 % of the subjects include dysgeusia, infusion site pain, diarrhea, hypotension, abdominal pain, nasopharyngitis, feeling hot, phlebitis, pyrexia, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, and injection site pain. The AEs experienced in phase 1 studies were similar to the AEs seen in the subsequent phase 3 studies. There are no significant safety issues or concerns based on the phase 1 data.
L3205: The pediatric phase 1 studies BPR-PIP-001 and CSI-1006 were multicenter, open-label, single-dose, add-on studies of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects undergoing treatment with IV antibacterial drugs with the aim of evaluating the single-dose PK and safety of ceftobiprole. Trial BPR-PIP-001 included 15 neonates and infants aged up to 3 months; 6 treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 6 subjects and only one TEAE of diaper dermatitis occurred in more than one subject. Neither the TEAEs nor the two SAEs of cerebral infarction and diaphragmatic hernia were considered to be related to the study drug. Study CSI-1006 included 64 subjects aged 3 months to less than 18 years. Eight subjects experienced 14 SAEs, none of which were considered treatment-related by the investigator. TEAEs were reported in 48.4% of subjects and vomiting was the most common (9.4%). TEAEs of vomiting, diaper dermatitis, pruritis, headache, increased eosinophil count, diarrhea, catheter-related site reaction, urine crystals, increased alanine aminotransferase (125 U/L), and increased aspartate aminotransferase (121 U/L) were considered potentially related to ceftobiprole; the latter two laboratory-based TEAEs occurred in the same subject. No deaths were reported and no subjects discontinued either Study due to a TEAE.

L3321: ## 18. Clinical Virology

L3323: ## 19. Clinical Microbiology
L3324: ## 19.1. In Vitro Activity
L3325: The in vitro ceftobiprole MIC range and concentrations required to inhibit 90% of isolates (\text{MIC}_{90}) against the target pathogen isolates collected in the JMI SENTRY surveillance studies from 2016 to 2020 and isolates collected in the European Union surveillance studies from 2016 to 2019 is shown in Table 288. Ceftobiprole is active against MSSA (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.5 mcg/mL), MRSA (\text{MIC}_{90} = 2 mcg/mL), *S. pneumoniae* (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.25-0.5 mcg/mL), *S. pyogenes* (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.015 mcg/mL), *S. agalactiae* (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.03 mcg/mL), *H. influenzae* (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.12 mcg/mL), and *H. parainfluenzae* (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.25 mcg/mL). The ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90}s for the penicillin-resistant *S. pneumoniae* subset was higher (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.5 mcg/mL) than for the penicillin-susceptible subset (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.015 mcg/mL) but were within the proposed susceptible breakpoint of \le 0.5 mcg/mL for ceftobiprole.
L3326: The ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90} for *E. faecalis* and *E. faecium* were 2 mcg/mL and &gt;4 mcg/mL, respectively. The ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90} against *M. catarrhalis* was 0.25 mcg/mL. Against 12 vancomycin-resistant/ampicillin-susceptible *E. faecalis*, the ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90} was 2 mcg/mL.
L3327: Ceftobiprole is active against some gram-negative bacteria producing AmpC cephalosporinases or non-ESBL Class A enzymes with \text{MIC}_{90} values of \le 1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole has limited activity against *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Acinetobacter* species with \text{MIC}_{90} values of \ge 16 mcg/mL. The ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90} values against *P. aeruginosa* are above the PK-PD target achievable by proposed dosing regimen. Ceftobiprole is not active against ESBL or metallo \beta-lactamases producing bacteria. The ceftobiprole \text{MIC}_{90}s for key pathogens, *S. aureus*, *S. pneumoniae*, *E. coli*, and *K. pneumoniae* isolates from the European Union surveillance were similar to that observed for the US isolates. Ceftobiprole, like other cephalosporins, is not active against the atypical intracellular bacterial CABP pathogens, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* or *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*. The ceftobiprole MIC against 30 *Legionella pneumophila* isolates by broth microdilution ranged from 0.03 – 0.12 mcg/mL (\text{MIC}_{90} = 0.06 mcg/mL) (Sahm 2007a). Ceftobiprole activity against intracellular forms of *L. pneumophila* has not been investigated. Ceftobiprole has limited activity against anaerobes.

L3346: ## 19.2. Interaction With Other Antimicrobials
L3347: In the *in vitro* checkerboard broth and/or time kill assays, ceftobiprole was tested in combination with daptomycin, vancomycin, gentamicin, or rifampin against 20 MRSA strains with varying degrees of vancomycin susceptibility. Ceftobiprole was also tested in combination with doripenem, levofloxacin or colistin against strains of *P. aeruginosa* (N = 24), *A. baumannii* (N = 19) or fluoroquinolone-resistant *E. coli* (N = 19). Ceftobiprole in combination with ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, amikacin, and tobramycin was evaluated in 61 clinical *P. aeruginosa* isolates. No antagonism was observed in these studies. Majority of the combination were indifferent.
L3348: ## 19.3. In Vivo Activity
L3349: The in vivo activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in multiple animal models of infection. These include the murine septicemia model, the murine peritonitis model, the neutropenic thigh infection model (PK-PD studies), the murine acute pneumonia model, the rat and rabbit endocarditis model, the rabbit meningitis model, the rat and rabbit osteomyelitis model, and the murine urinary tract infection model.
L3350: ## Murine Septicemia Model
L3351: Ceftobiprole (ED_{50} values &lt;5 mg/kg) was effective in treating experimental septicemia in mice due to *S. aureus* strains (ceftobiprole MIC values \le 2 mcg/mL) (Table 290). Against MRSA I-6 and MRSA 8525, ceftobiprole was more active than vancomycin (vancomycin ED_{50} = 6.7 mg/kg and 12.1 mg/kg). Ceftobiprole also demonstrated activity against three penicillin-resistant strains of *S. pneumoniae*, including a strain *S. pneumoniae* 23 F-CTR (ceftobiprole MIC 1 mg/mL), however, the ceftobiprole ED_{50} for the *S. pneumoniae* penicillin resistant strains were higher than the *S. pneumoniae* penicillin sensitive strain. Similar ceftobiprole doses (ED_{50} &lt;5 mg/kg) were effective against *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, *C. freundii*, *S. marcescens* and *P. mirabilis*. Against the TEM-1 containing *E. coli* OC4367, the ceftobiprole ED_{50} was higher (2.7 mg/kg/day) than against the parent *E. coli* strain (0.5 mg/kg/day) but ceftobiprole was more active than ceftazidime or cefepime and as active as meropenem. The presence of the ACT-1 AmpC cephalosporinase did not affect the in vivo activity of the ceftobiprole and comparators in this animal model. The strain *Proteus vulgaris* 1028 with *in vitro* resistance to ceftobiprole was also resistant in vivo (ED_{50} &gt;12 mg/kg). Cefepime (ED_{50} = 1 mg/kg) and meropenem (ED_{50} &lt;0.4 mg/kg) had greater activity against the *P. aeruginosa* BA strain compared to ceftobiprole (ED_{50} = 4 mg/kg).

L3359: ## **Murine Peritonitis Model**
L3360: In the murine peritonitis model, female mice were infected intraperitoneally with *E. faecalis* (10X the 50% lethal dose) and then immediately treated subcutaneously with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium or ampicillin. Against the rare \beta-lactamase-producing strain TX0921, ceftobiprole was more active than ampicillin (Table 291). It is likely that the activity of ceftobiprole against \beta-lactamase-producing *E. faecalis* is due to the inherent stability of the drug to hydrolysis by this enzyme (similar to class A staphylococcal penicillinase PC1). Ceftobiprole PD50 (dose that protects 50% of the animals) values at 96 hours were lower than ampicillin for *E. faecalis* strains TX2484, and OG1RF, respectively.

L3368: ## **Murine Acute Pneumonia Model**
L3369: In the immunocompromised murine model of acute pneumonia, the ten-day cumulative survival rates for infected mice (all strains) receiving ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (total daily doses of ceftobiprole equivalents, 2.1 to 75 mg/kg) ranged from 57 to 100%, whereas with ceftriaxone (total daily doses, 10 to 400 mg/kg), the survival rates varied between 13 and 100% (Table 292). In the immunocompetent murine model of acute pneumonia, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium reduced bacterial burden in the lungs. Against the wildtype strain ATCC 6301, and the two macrolide-resistant isolates, the ceftobiprole ED_{50} was 2.5- to 4-fold lower than that determined for ceftriaxone. Against *H. influenzae*, *E. cloacae* and the non-ESBL producing *K. pneumoniae* ceftobiprole, ceftriaxone and cefepime all reduced bacterial burden in the lungs compared to no treatment. The reason for the activity of ceftriaxone (MIC=16 mcg/mL; Intermediate susceptibility) against the non-ESBL producing *K. pneumoniae* is not clear. For the ESBL-positive *K. pneumoniae* strain where the MICs were all greater than or equal to 128 mcg/mL, there was no difference between treated and untreated animals. Emergence of resistance studies conducted on bacteria recovered after therapy (except for ESBL-positive *K. pneumoniae*) found post-treatment MIC values within 2-fold of pre-treatment MIC values.

L3376: ## Neutropenic murine thigh infection model
L3377: The neutropenic murine thigh infection model was used for PK-PD assessments and ceftobiprole exposures for a 1 log kill for *S. aureus* (MRSA and MSSA), *S. pneumoniae*, *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae*, *E. cloacae* were determined (see section 19.4).
L3378: ## Endocarditis Model
L3379: The activity of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium against *S. aureus* was examined in a rat and rabbit model of endocarditis (Table 293). In the rat model of endocarditis, the three ceftobiprole medocaril sodium dosing regimens (72 mg/kg, 144 mg/kg, and 288 mg/kg that achieved steady-state levels in serum of 2.5, 5, and 10 times the MIC for the test organisms) cleared &gt;90% of vegetations in rats with experimental endocarditis caused by penicillinase-producing MRSA COL (Bla+) and the MRSA P8-Hom strain. Blood and spleen cultures from all animals were negative. No resistant mutants were isolated from infected vegetations from any group of treated
L3380: animals. In another study, treatment with standard dose-ceftobiprole simulating human kinetics of 500 mg every 12 hours (q12h) cleared 93% and 77% of vegetations infected with strains PC3 and Mu50, respectively, and reduced the vegetation counts by &gt;6 \log_{10} CFU/g compared to those in untreated controls. In general, spleens remained infected even after effective antibacterial therapy of the valves with some decrease in the bacterial burden. After 3 days of treatment, rats were followed for an additional three days without drug for relapse. In the relapse subset, regrowth of bacteria was observed with all treatment groups.
L3381: In the rabbit model of endocarditis, the activity of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (25 mg/kg (equivalent to 19 mg of ceftobiprole per kg) intramuscularly every 8 hours for 4 days) was equivalent to that of vancomycin (30 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours for 4 days) in rabbits infected with MRSA 76, and superior to that of vancomycin for rabbits infected with the vancomycin-intermediate *Staphylococcus aureus* strain HIP5836. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (25 mg/kg intramuscular q8h for 4 days) cleared the vegetations, spleen and kidneys of MRSA in 6/7, 5/7, and 7/7 rabbits with aortic catheter infected with 1.5 \times 10^7 CFU of MRSA strain COL. In contrast, vancomycin (30 mg/kg intravenous q12h for 4 days) and daptomycin (18 mg/kg intravenous q24h for 4 days) cleared MRSA from these tissues in fewer animals.

L3390: ## **Rabbit Meningitis Model**
L3391: In the rabbit model of experimental meningitis, the activity of ceftobiprole (40 mg/kg IV once) was similar to cefepime (100 mg/kg at 0 and 4 hours) against *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae* and the \beta-lactamase-negative and positive *H. influenzae* strains (Table 294). Ceftobiprole reduced the bacterial burden in the CSF of animals infected with the \beta-lactamase-positive *H. influenzae* strain to a greater extent than cefepime.

L3398: ## **Rat and Rabbit Osteomyelitis Model**
L3399: In the rat model of MRSA mediastinitis and sternal osteomyelitis (Table 294), ceftobiprole (70 and 100 mg/kg for 5 days) decreased the MRSA load in the sternum by 1 \log_{10} and 1.4 \log_{10} compared with untreated controls and the vancomycin-treated group. MRSA was recovered from the spleen in 5/7 saline-treated animals but in none of the antibacterial drug-treated animals. Following 14 days therapy, 5/8 ceftobiprole-treated rats and 6/8 vancomycin-treated rats cleared MRSA from the sternum compared with none of the saline-treated animals. In those animals that did not clear MRSA, only rare colonies were recovered. In rabbits with localized osteomyelitis due to MRSA 168-1, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (40 mg/kg ceftobiprole equivalent, q8h, 4 weeks) administered subcutaneously was more active than vancomycin (30 mg/kg, q12h, 4 weeks, subcutaneous) or oral linezolid (60 mg/kg, q8h, 4 weeks) at 2 weeks after end of treatment.
L3400: ## **Murine Urinary Tract Infection Model**
L3401: In the murine urinary tract infection model, mice were treated with single doses of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (equivalent to 4.3 to 34.2 mg/kg of ceftobiprole and concentrations achievable in humans with standard human dosing) or vancomycin (2-fold range from 6.25 to 50 mg/kg of body weight), 1-hour post-infection. Two doses of ampicillin (2-fold range from 12.5 to 200 mg/kg) were administered subcutaneously 1- and 2-hour post-infection (previously shown to simulate ampicillin human doses of 3 gm). The minimum detection limit of bacteria in these experiments was 102 CFU/gm. Protection was defined as no recovery of bacteria from kidney or bladder homogenates at 48 hours post-infection. The authors state that ceftobiprole was active against the Bla+ and Bla- *E. faecalis* OG1 strains, while ampicillin (depending on the inoculum) was less effective against Bla+ than Bla- OG1 strains in this murine urinary tract infection model based on 50% protective dose (Table 295). However, it should be noted that treatment was initiated 1-2 hours post-infection making it difficult to assess if urinary tract infection was established. Hence, data from this Study should be interpreted with caution.

L3407: In summary, ceftobiprole was shown to be active against MSSA and MRSA in the murine septicemia model and rat and rabbit endocarditis and osteomyelitis models. Ceftobiprole was active against *S. pneumoniae*, including penicillin resistant strains in the murine septicemia and the murine acute pneumonia models. Ceftobiprole was also shown to be active against *E. coli* expressing TEM-1 and Act-1 AmpC cephalosporinase, *K. pneumoniae*, *C. freundii*, *S. marcescens*, and *P. mirabilis* in the murine septicemia model. In a rabbit model of meningitis ceftobiprole was effective at reducing bacterial burden in the CSF in rabbits infected with strains of *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae* and \beta-lactamase positive and negative *H. influenzae*. In both a rat and rabbit model of endocarditis, ceftobiprole did not sterilize but was effective in reducing cardiac vegetations of MRSA including a vancomycin intermediate strain. Similarly, in both a rat and rabbit model of osteomyelitis, ceftobiprole was effective in reducing bacterial burden in MRSA infected sternal bones.
L3408: ## 19.4. PK/PD Studies
L3409: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies in the neutropenic mouse thigh infection model identified %fT&gt;MIC as the PK/PD index that correlated with *in vivo* activity. An exposure target of %fT&gt;MIC = 30% for 1-log kill was selected based on the animal studies with gram-positive bacteria (Table 296 and Table 297).

L3432: PK/PD target attainment analysis was conducted using data from the completed phase 1, 2 and 3 studies. L3433: ## 19.5. Clinical Studies
L3434: ## *Staphylococcus aureus* Bacteremia
L3435: BPR-CS-009 was a randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial conducted to establish the efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium compared to daptomycin in the treatment of SAB, including infective endocarditis. The trial assessed microbiological eradication rates (negative blood culture for *S. aureus*) at Day 4, Day 8, and the EOT and PTE visits in the mITT population. The mITT population comprised of 387 subjects (ceftobiprole: n = 189; comparator: n = 198). In the ceftobiprole group, 74.6% of subjects (141/189) had an MSSA infection at baseline, and 23.8% of subjects (45/189) had an MRSA infection at baseline. In the comparator group, 73.7% of subjects (146/198) had an MSSA infection, and 24.7% of subjects (49/198) had an MRSA infection.
L3436: The microbiological eradication rates at various visits in the mITT population in subjects with SAB due to MSSA and MRSA are shown in Table 299. The microbiological eradication rates appear to be slightly lower in the MRSA subgroup compared to the MSSA subgroup but could be due to the small number of subjects with MRSA.

L3457: ## ABSSSIs
L3458: Trial BPR-CS-008 was a double-blind, non-inferiority, active-controlled trial, which randomized 679 adult subjects with qualifying ABSSSI and who fulfilled the requirement to receive intravenous antibacterial drugs in a hospital setting. The mITT population consisted of 506 subjects (ceftobiprole N= 244; vancomycin plus aztreonam N =262) and was a subset of subjects in the ITT population who had causative pathogens identified by the central microbiology laboratory from skin lesions or blood cultures. Local laboratory results were included only if isolate could not be cultured at the central laboratory. Nine gram-negative and 27 gram-positive baseline pathogens isolated from subjects in the mITT population were only analyzed by local laboratories. The ME population consisted of 426 subjects (ceftobiprole N= 203; vancomycin plus aztreonam N =223) and was the subset of subjects in the mITT population who were also in the clinically evaluable population. Gram-positive pathogens were isolated at Baseline in 442 subjects while gram-negative pathogens were isolated in 34 subjects and mixed gram positive and gram-negative pathogens were isolated in 30 subjects at Baseline. The early clinical response and investigator's assessment of overall clinical success at TOC by Baseline pathogen are shown in Table 302. Ceftobiprole was active against *S. aureus* (methicillin sensitive and methicillin resistant), *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and *K. pneumoniae*. There were no ABSSSI subjects with baseline *E. coli* in the mITT population. It should be noted that the number of subjects with *Enterobacter cloacae* was small (n = 3), but all 3 subjects were a clinical success, including a subject with *E. cloacae* isolate with MIC&gt;64 mcg/mL (Table 303).

L3475: ## Bacteremia Subjects
L3476: Of the 506 subjects in the mITT population, 17 (3.4%) had concomitant bacteremia and had pathogens isolated from baseline blood cultures. Of the 17 subjects with positive blood cultures, 7 were in the ceftobiprole arm and 10 were in the comparator arm). All subjects with positive blood cultures in the ceftobiprole arm (n = 7) were responders, while 9 out of 10 subjects were responders in the comparator arm (Table 304).

L3494: ## Increase in MIC (≥4 Fold)
L3495: Only one subject in the ceftobiprole arm, Subject [REDACTED](b) (6), had a pathogen with a ≥ 4-fold increase in the ceftobiprole MIC. The pathogen was *E. faecalis* with a baseline ceftobiprole MIC of 0.25 mcg/mL that increased to 8 mcg/mL at EOT. Even though this subject had a microbiological persistence at EOT, the subject met the definition of clinical cure. The isolate was not further characterized.
L3496: ## CABP
L3497: Common typical bacterial pathogens that cause CABP include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. Atypical bacterial pathogens such as *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, and *Legionella pneumophila* also cause CABP. Data from two multiregional phase 3 trials, CAP-3001 and BPR-PIP-002 were included to support the CABP indication. Evidence of efficacy and safety in HABP from trial BPR 248/307 was included to provide additional information on the pneumonia population. The Applicant is not requesting an indication for the treatment of HABP and data from this trial were not reviewed for efficacy.

L3535: ## Increase in MIC

L3546: ## 19.6. In Vitro Susceptibility Test Method
L3547: The MIC values for ceftobiprole were determined by broth microdilution method in accordance with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (M07-A6). Tier 1 studies evaluated the effect of media (cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, Iso-Sensitest broth), media supplementation (25 mg/L calcium, 0.002% Tween 80), temperature (30°C or 35°C), presence of 2% NaCl, inoculum size, incubation conditions (5%CO2), pH, and serum. A 2-fold increase in ceftobiprole MICs against the two *P. aeruginosa* strains occurred with increase of inoculum density from 104 to 105 to 106 CFU/mL. Increases in ceftobiprole MIC were also made when high inoculum \beta-lactamase-positive strains were tested. Ceftobiprole MIC values from dry-form broth microdilution MIC panels were within 1log2 dilution of the reference frozen-form MIC values. Overall, the ceftobiprole MIC obtained under various of testing conditions were within 1log2 dilution of the standard CLSI broth microdilution method.
L3548: ## Quality Control for Reference Broth Microdilution
L3549: Tier 2 studies were conducted in 8 laboratories and utilized the frozen-form reference broth microdilution panels prepared by [REDACTED](b) (4) and four lots of cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth. The quality control (QC) strains and ranges for broth microdilution susceptibility testing of ceftobiprole have been published (CLSI 2005) (Table 313).

L3554: ## **Ceftobiprole Disk Diffusion Method**
L3555: The 30 mcg ceftobiprole disk, similar to other cephalosporin disk masses, was originally developed according to CLSI M23 guidelines and QC ranges were established by CLSI (CLSI M23). Since the original disk development studies, a new 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk was found to reduce the size of the inhibition zones and was commercialized in the European regions.
L3556: ## **Disk Optimization**
L3557: The activity of the 5 (lot#322789), 10 (lot# 322790), and 30 (lot# 322793) mcg ceftobiprole disks against seven QC strains (*E. coli* ATCC® 25922, *H. influenzae* ATCC® 49247, *H. influenzae* NCTC 8468, *P. aeruginosa* ATCC® 27853, *S. aureus* ATCC® 25923, *S. aureus* ATCC® 29213, *S. pneumoniae* ATCC® 49619) was examined using [REDACTED] disk (Technical report CT-041). All 3 disk masses resulted in an acceptable zone size range (i.e., a variation of not more than 3 mm) for all QC strains tested. A study conducted by the EUCAST laboratory examined 5 mcg (from [REDACTED]) and 30 mcg ceftobiprole disks against 40 – 42 clinical isolates each of *S. aureus*, *S. pneumoniae* (including a penicillin non-susceptible subset), and different species of the *Enterobacteriales*. Scatterplots comparing the 30 mcg and 5 mcg disks using the raw data provided by the EUCAST laboratory was submitted. The 5 mcg ceftobiprole disks was stated to result in a better differentiation for non-wildtype isolates than the 30 mcg disks.
L3558: ## **Disk Stability**
L3559: Stability study was conducted using [REDACTED] (b) (4) 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk (Study 9294). Three batches were tested (Batches 011321087, 101421109 and 111221068). The data suggests that the [REDACTED] (b) (4) 5 mcg ceftobiprole disks were stable for 21 months at -20 \pm 5^{\circ}\text{C} / 5 \pm 3^{\circ}\text{C} and under in-use condition of 5 \pm 3^{\circ}\text{C} for 7 days. The disk stability study performed by [REDACTED] (b) (4) suggest that their 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk (lot #322793) was stable for 4 weeks at -20^{\circ}\text{C} and 4^{\circ}\text{C} (Technical report CT-041).
L3560: ## Disk Diffusion QC Strains And Ranges
L3561: A study (3422 2020) was conducted in seven laboratories using three media lots (different manufacturers), two disk lots (lot# 435540), and lot#90319080 and 420 test points to establish disk diffusion QC ranges for a 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk against two QC organisms recommended by CLSI: *E. coli* ATCC 25922 and *S. aureus* ATCC 25923. The QC ranges were approved by CLSI in August 2020 (Table 314).

L3581: ## *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
L3582: The assessment supports a ceftobiprole susceptible breakpoint of 0.5 mcg/mL for *S. pneumoniae* based on MIC90 values, animal studies with isolates with MIC of 1 mcg/mL, PK-PD target attainment, clinical cure rates in the CABP trial (Table 317). Limited clinical data at MIC of 1 mcg/mL. L3617: ## 20. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance
L3618: ## 20.1. Mechanism of Action
L3619: Ceftobiprole exerts its antibacterial activity by binding to multiple penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibiting their transpeptidase activity, which is essential for the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall. The concentrations required to inhibit 50% binding to PBPs (IC_{50s}) from various gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria were determined using fluorescein-labeled penicillin, [H^3]-penicillin, biocillin fluorescein-labeled, or fluorescein isothiocyanate labeled ampicillin (Table 322 and Table 323). The studies showed that ceftobiprole has a high affinity for *S. aureus* PBPs 1 – 4, including PBP2a in methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (Table 322). Ceftobiprole has high affinity for all six *S. pneumoniae* PBPs in penicillin-susceptible strains, including PBP2b. Ceftobiprole's PBP binding affinity is reduced for PBP1b and PBP2b in penicillin-resistant strains, but ceftobiprole still has good affinity for PBP1a, PBP2a, PBP2x, and PBP3 in these strains. Ceftobiprole has a high affinity for *S. epidermidis* PBP 2', compared to all other \beta-lactams measured. Ceftobiprole has good affinity for wildtype PBPs 1-5 of *E. faecium* but does not have measurable affinity for the mutated PBP5 from ampicillin-resistant *E. faecium*, resulting in elevated \beta-lactam MICs in *E. faecium* strains that have these variants of PBP5.

## Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
L3638: In *E.coli*, ceftobiprole has good affinity for PBP3 and PBP2. The ceftobiprole IC_{50s} for PBP1a and PBP4 were similar to ceftriaxone and imipenem (Table 323). In *P. aeruginosa*, ceftobiprole, ceftazidime, and imipenem had comparable binding affinities for PBP1a and PBP3. Incubation of *P. aeruginosa* strain PAO-1 or *E. coli* MC4100 for 2 hours in the presence of 1x MIC of ceftobiprole led to filamentation (Davies 2007a, Glen 2021). The IC_{50} and filamentation data, indicate that PBP3 is the preferred target in gram-negative bacilli. Ceftobiprole has high affinity for purified PBP1b from *C. freundii*, which is comparable to ceftriaxone.

L3647: Ceftobiprole is a poor substrate for class C \beta-lactamases and is hydrolyzed at very low rates (Table 324). Ceftobiprole is also a poor substrate for class A enzymes, particularly penicillinases (e.g., *S. aureus* PC1). It is readily hydrolyzed by the class A cephalosporinase from *P. vulgaris* 1028 and by ESBLs (TEM derivatives).

L3653: Ceftobiprole was hydrolyzed slowly by the common staphylococcal PC1 \beta-lactamase, the class A TEM-1 \beta-lactamase, and the class C AmpC \beta-lactamase but was labile to hydrolysis by class B, class D, and class A extended-spectrum \beta-lactamases (Table 325). Ceftobiprole and cefepime generally had lower MICs than ceftazidime for AmpC producing organisms, particularly AmpC-overexpressing *Enterobacter cloacae* organisms. However, all three cephalosporins were hydrolyzed very slowly by AmpC cephalosporinases. Strains producing derepressed AmpC or rare class A cephalosporinases or strains producing ESBLs have higher ceftobiprole MICs, confirming that ceftobiprole is hydrolyzed by these enzymes.

L3680: ## 20.2. Mechanism of Resistance
L3681: Single-step resistance frequencies were determined for 10 *S. aureus* strains using agar plates containing ceftobiprole at 2x to 8x MIC and an inoculum of 5 x 108 to 5 x 109 CFU. Resistance frequencies observed for ceftobiprole were low in *S. aureus* and ranged from ~9.6 x 10-8 at 2x MIC to &lt;1.5 x 10-10 at 8X MIC (Table 326). In serial passage studies, a 4-fold increase in MIC was observed in 3 out of 5 *S. aureus* isolates after 50 passages. In the case of coagulase negative
L3682: staphylococci, the ceftobiprole resistance frequencies were 1.1 \times 10^{-8} to &lt;7.7 \times 10^{-10} and 4 of the 5 strains had a 4-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages. In most cases, the transiently elevated ceftobiprole MICs decreased when the strains were cultured in the absence of drug, suggesting the resistance mutations were not stable.
L3683: When a high inoculum of *S. aureus* strains (10^9 CFU/mL) was serially passaged in subinhibitory concentrations of ceftobiprole for 28 days, resistance due to rare mutations developed in 20-21 days. For the strain carrying mutated *mecA* gene on a plasmid with an initial ceftobiprole MIC of 16 mcg/mL, the MIC increased to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. For the strain carrying wildtype *mecA* gene on a plasmid in a *mecA*- background, ceftobiprole MIC increased from 4 mcg/mL to 128 mcg/mL after 21 passages. In the third strain that lacked the *mecA* gene, ceftobiprole MIC increased from 1 mcg/mL to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. The *mecA* gene acquired mutations which lie close to the ceftobiprole binding site (Banerjee et al. 2008). The mutations in the *mecA*- strain that led to an increased ceftobiprole MIC were in three genes: two substitutions were in the gene encoding the low molecular weight PBP4, one in a gene encoding a predicted signaling protein, GdpP, and one in the gene encoding an efflux protein, AcrB, which is implicated in resistance to cationic compounds.
L3684: Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 10 *S. pneumoniae* (including penicillin sensitive and penicillin resistant) strains ranged from 2 \times 10^{-7} at 2x MIC to &lt;6.7 \times 10^{-9} at 8X MIC. Three strains showed a 2-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages.
L3685: Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 8 *H. influenzae* (including \beta lactamase positive and \beta lactamase negative) and 2 *M. catarrhalis* strains resulted in very low resistance frequencies of &lt;4.3 \times 10^{-11} to 1.3 \times 10^{-10} at 2x MIC and 8x MIC. A 4-fold increase in MIC was seen in one strain after 50 passages.
L3686: Single-step mutants were obtained by exposing clinical isolates of *Morganella morganii*, *Citrobacter freundii*, *Providencia stuartii*, *Enterobacter cloacae*, *Serratia marcescens*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* to 2x-, 4x- and 8x- ceftobiprole MICs. Single-step resistance frequencies for five *Enterobacteriales* strains and one *P. aeruginosa* strain were 10^{-6} to 10^{-8} at 2x MIC for ceftobiprole and comparable to the values obtained for cefepime and ceftazidime. The resistant mutants in *C. freundii* and *E. cloacae* occurred at frequencies of 10^{-6} at 2x MIC and 4x MIC of ceftobiprole. The mutants appeared to have become resistant through over-expression of the chromosomal Class C \beta-lactamase. Mutants of *P. aeruginosa* were obtained at a frequency of 10^{-6} and &lt;10^{-9} at 2x MIC and 4x MIC, respectively. None of the mutants over-expressed the chromosomal Class C \beta-lactamase but were found to over-express the MexXY efflux pump (Queenan et al. 2010). The mutation frequencies for *Enterobacteriales* and *P. aeruginosa* were higher than those observed for *S. aureus* and *S. pneumoniae*.

L3691: ## **Resistance in Isolates From Ceftobiprole Clinical Trials**
L3692: In the CAP-3001 (CABP) trial, *K. pneumoniae* isolates from 1 subject had a \ge 4-fold increase in the ceftobiprole MICs between baseline (0.12 mcg/mL) and post-baseline (&gt;16 mcg/mL). The organism acquired an ESBL (TEM-4 with 4 amino acid changes) (Queenan 2009d). The Applicant concluded that ceftobiprole resistance did not develop over the course of therapy and the subject was infected with a new strain of *K. pneumoniae* which had a higher ceftobiprole MICs and expressed more resistance mechanisms.
L3693: Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with a \ge 4-fold increase in ceftobiprole MIC values were characterized by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (Queenan 2009b). Eleven subjects had related or identical isolates post-baseline with increased ceftobiprole MICs analysis. All 11 baseline isolates were gram-negative (*P. aeruginosa*, n=4; *A. baumannii*, n=2; *E. cloacae*, n = 2; *E. coli*, n = 1; *S. marcescens*, n = 1; and *K. pneumoniae*, n = 1). The pulsed-field gel electrophoresis results suggest that resistance to ceftobiprole developed while on therapy for these isolates. Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with ceftobiprole MIC values \ge 16 mcg/mL were evaluated for the expression of \beta-lactamases. Three principal resistance profiles were discovered: (1) ESBL-positive, with CTX-M or SHV family Class A extended-spectrum \beta-lactamases, (2) ESBL-positive, combined with an AmpC Class C \beta-lactamase, (3) ESBL-negative, having an AmpC Class C \beta-lactamase, either plasmid-encoded or chromosomally located. Ceftobiprole is not active against gram-negative bacteria producing ESBLs from TEM, SHV or CTX-M families, serine carbapenemases (such as KPC), class B metallo-\beta-lactamases, or class C (AmpC cephalosporinases) expressed at high levels and Ambler class D \beta-lactamases including carbapenemases.
L3694: In summary, resistance in some bacteria is due to poor binding to PBPs, expression of \beta lactamases including AmpC \beta lactamases, and expression of efflux pumps. In *E. faecium*, \beta-lactam resistance is mediated by low affinity binding to PBP5, which may be expressed at higher levels in ampicillin-resistant isolates. Ceftobiprole is resistant to hydrolysis by *S. aureus* penicillinases and is hydrolyzed slowly by some Class C and Class A \beta-lactamases found in gram-negative bacteria. Like most cephalosporins, ceftobiprole is hydrolyzed by ESBLs, serine carbapenemases and metallo-\beta-lactamases. It is also hydrolyzed by the Class A cephalosporinases from *Proteus vulgaris*, which has inherent resistance to ceftobiprole.
L3695: ## **Cross-Resistance**
L3696: Analysis of drug-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* subset of the 2016-2020 SENTRY surveillance isolates demonstrated that ceftobiprole was active against isolates non-susceptible to clindamycin, daptomycin, erythromycin, gentamicin, levofloxacin, linezolid, tetracycline, tigecycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (ceftobiprole susceptibility ranged from 97.7%–100.0% based on the proposed ceftobiprole breakpoint of S \le 2 mcg/mL for *S. aureus*). Ceftobiprole MIC50/90 values (e.g., 0.5/2 mcg/mL) were identical for the *S. aureus* subsets with vancomycin MIC values of \le 1 mcg/mL and &gt;1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole maintained activity against 88.0% of the ceftaroline non-susceptible isolates.

Product Quality Sections (i.e., DOSAGE FORMS AND STRENGTHS, DESCRIPTION, HOW SUPPLIED/STORAGE AND HANDLING)	
In the Dosage Forms and Strengths Section (3) of the PI, the strength was presented in terms of the salt (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium instead of the prodrug (ceftobiprole medocaril) and the active metabolite (ceftobiprole). This was an exception to the salt policy in the Guidance for Industry: Naming of Drug Products Containing Salt Drug Substances. This strength presentation was also included in Section 11 Description and Section 16 How Supplied/Storage and Handling of the PI. In the Description Section (11) of the PI, the sodium content stated as "Each vial of ZEVTERA contains approximately 32 mg of sodium" was added as per the labeling recommendations in the Draft Guidance for Industry: Quantitative Labeling of Sodium, Potassium, and Phosphorus for Human Over-the-Counter and Prescription Drug Products.
Refer to the Office of Product Quality Assessment (in DARRTS dated 3/28/2024) for additional details regarding the labeling changes to the product quality sections.

L3909: Flowchart detailing the Trial Schema, CAP-3001.
Screening leads to Eligibility:
\ge 18 years of age
CAP severe enough to require hospitalization (PSI \le 90 versus PSI \ge 91) and treatment with i.v. antibiotics for at least 3 days (72 hours)
If YES, proceed to Randomization (Day 1)a. If NO, proceed to Ineligible.
Randomization leads to the Double-Blind Treatment Phase.
Days 1-10b treatment options:
Arm 1 (Left):
Ceftobiprole 500 mg in 250 mL D5W as a 120-minute i.v. infusion every 8 hours
Placebo of 50 mL D5W as a 30-minute i.v. infusion every 24 hours
+/- Placebo of 300 mL normal saline (NaCl 0.9% solution) as a 60-minute i.v. infusion every 12 hoursc
Arm 2 (Right):
Comparator (Ceftriaxone) 2 g in 50 mL D5W as a 30-minute i.v. infusion every 24 hours
Placebo of 250 mL D5W as a 120-minute i.v. infusion every 8 hours (normal saline used when linezolid was added)
+/- Linezolid 600 mg in 300 mL D5W as a 60-minute i.v. infusion every 12 hoursc
Both arms proceed to Optional switch to oral cefuroxime axetil 500 mg every 12 hours, for subjects who meet the protocol defined criteria after \ge 3 days (72 hours) of i.v. study drug therapy.
This leads to Days 10-14d treatment:
Optional Prolonged Treatment with or without optional i.v. to oral switch
Followed by End-of-Treatment Within 48 hours after the end of therapy.
Followed by Follow-up Phase.
Followed by Test-of-Cure/Early Termination 7 to 14 days after last dose of study drug.
Followed by Late Follow-Upe 28 to 35 days after last dose of study drug.
L3910: Flowchart illustrating the disposition of subjects in Trial CAP-3001.
The process starts with CAP3001 Total Enrollment (N = 706).
From Total Enrollment, subjects were either Screen Failures (N = 40) or Removed from ITT (N = 28, 14 Each Group).
The remaining subjects formed the Randomized ITT (N = 638).
The Randomized ITT population was split into two arms:
Ceftobiprole (N = 314):Clinically Evaluable (N = 231)
Safety (N = 310)
mITT (N = 87)

Comparator (N = 324):Clinically Evaluable (N = 238)
Safety (N = 322)
mITT (N = 97)

Both mITT groups (N = 87 and N = 97) were further evaluated for Microbiologically Evaluable subjects (N = 68 and N = 76, respectively).
